questions: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right?

lines.short: Not always: several deaths blamed on it in the news had other causes.
lines.but: One study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.
how: From late 2009 to around April 2011, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone.
Later reports said mephedrone was not found in 4, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses.
The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone.
Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news. The author thinks the news raised interest in the drug, but search data cannot show that the news made people use it.

cards.statement: The two UK deaths most linked to mephedrone in online news were later found to be from alcohol and methadone.
Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths linked to it were in the news, one study found.

questions: Was mephedrone actually found in the deaths blamed on it?

lines.short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.
lines.but: A positive test does not prove cause. A negative test may miss earlier use.
how: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone; 13 results were still pending.
Of 62 deaths studied, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. Other drugs were common.
One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death. Their earlier test evidence is not given.
The authors say tests and incomplete reporting may also miss deaths. They cannot give a death rate.

cards.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.

questions: Is ecstasy really MDMA, and how strong are the pills?

lines.short: Often, but not always. In European pill tests in 2009, 19 to 64 in 100 pills held MDMA, depending on the country. By 2013 most did, and held more of it.
lines.but: These were pills people chose to bring in, and the newest tests are from 2013. Pills today may be different.
how: A 2004 review of pill tests found MDMA in 90 to 98 in 100 ecstasy pills from the 1980s to the early 1990s, 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. Others held related drugs, other things such as ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active.

Drug-checking services in five European countries tested pills people brought in, from 2008 to 2013. Pills holding MDMA dropped in 2009, to about 19 in 100 in Austria and 64 in 100 in the Netherlands, then mostly recovered. Newer drugs such as mCPP or PMMA turned up in some ecstasy.

The MDMA in a pill ranged from none to about 150 mg in older tests. Where measured, the average rose from about 61 to 74 mg in 2009 to about 103 to 114 mg in 2013: nearly double in the Netherlands, less elsewhere. These are lab measurements, not amounts to take.

Some people feel little from a pill, and some then take more. A weaker pill, or one with no MDMA, is one possible reason; in an Australian survey, people thought about 1 pill in 4 or 5 was a dud. Neither source looked at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more.

cards.statement: Pills sold as ecstasy have nearly always held MDMA.

questions: Do benzo test strips catch etizolam and other newer benzos?

lines.short: Not reliably. At drug-checking sites in Canada, strips caught newer benzos in 15 of 24 samples that had them, and just 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.
lines.but: A lab checked only some samples, not chosen at random: some were picked because of a suspected benzo overdose.
how: At eight health sites, samples were tested with strips, and a lab checked some of them.
Strips caught 7 of 8 samples with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam. With etizolam alone, they caught only 8 of 16.
They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which the lab found none; what set those off wasn't reported.
The same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam, even at 40 or more times the level at which it caught other benzos. An earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up.

cards.statement: A negative benzodiazepine test strip means a drug has no newer benzodiazepines in it.

questions: What can drug-checking strips and colour kits not tell you?

lines.short: A test for one drug did not show other drugs in the mix, or how much.
lines.but: Only two small studies tested this directly. The rest is how the tests are made.
how: In one lab study, MDMA samples with caffeine or amphetamine mixed in looked the same on a colour test.
At one drug-checking service, 24 of 159 samples checked by a lab had a newer benzodiazepine. None of the people who brought them expected it. Most also had fentanyl.
Fentanyl strips only show if fentanyl is there. They do not show how much.
No study tested whether a negative result makes a drug less risky.

cards.statement: At one drug-checking service, nobody who brought a sample with a newer benzodiazepine expected it to be there.

questions: What is levamisole in cocaine, and what harm can it do?

lines.short: An animal worm medicine often found in cocaine, linked to blood and skin harm.
lines.but: This comes from case reports, so how often it causes harm is unknown.
how: Around 2010 it was in about 7 in 10 cocaine samples tested by US drug police, and in 8 or 9 in 10 urine samples that tested positive for cocaine in two US cities.
In some people the white blood cells that fight infection fell very low. Counts came back 5 to 10 days after the exposure stopped, or sooner with a hospital medicine.
Others had painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin, often on the ears, cheeks or nose. Most healed within weeks of stopping cocaine, but some needed skin grafts or amputation.
Cases were linked to levamisole mainly because the person used cocaine. Since most cocaine held it, finding it shows a person was exposed, not that it caused the harm.

cards.statement: Around 2010, most cocaine tested by US drug police contained an animal worm medicine.
Levamisole, an animal worm medicine often found in cocaine around 2010, has been linked to blood and skin harm.

questions: Are fake pills with fentanyl getting more common?

lines.short: Yes, in US records to 2021. Overdose deaths with signs of fake pills rose from 2 to about 5 in 100, and to about 15 in 100 in western states.
lines.but: These are police and death records, which can't show what share of street pills hold fentanyl. Death records likely miss many fake pills.
how: US police records: of seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021. The rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months rose from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million.

Death records from 29 states and Washington, DC: deaths with signs of fake pills went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to a high of about 5 in 100 in mid-2021, then stayed near there. In western states, about 5 became about 15 in 100.

In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes in 93 in 100.
Neither record shows how much fentanyl the pills held or what else was in them, and death records don't say how many pills were tested. A drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say.

cards.statement: By late 2021, about 15 in 100 overdose deaths in the western US showed signs of fake pills.
In US overdose deaths with signs of fake pills, most involved fake oxycodone.

questions: What does meth do in the brain?

lines.short: It makes nerve cells let out three brain chemicals: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
lines.but: How it does this is not fully known. So far we have only read a review about it.
how: Meth makes nerve endings let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
It seems to push them out of their storage sacs and run their pumps in reverse.
The details are not fully known. This comes from a review; we have not read the lab studies yet.

cards.statement: Meth seems to make nerve cells' chemical pumps run in reverse, pushing brain chemicals out.

questions: Do the two mirror-image forms of meth act differently?

lines.short: Yes: in one study, the 'l' form felt weaker and its effects ended sooner.
lines.but: One small lab study of injected doses in 12 men.
how: Meth comes in two mirror-image forms; which one depends on how it was made.
In 12 men, the 'l' form stayed in the blood longer but felt weaker and shorter.
It also raised blood pressure less.
One small study of injected doses, in men only.

cards.statement: Meth comes in two mirror-image forms, and which form it is depends on how it was made.

questions: Do the two mirror-image forms of ketamine, S and R, do different things?

lines.short: In one small study the S form caused psychosis-like effects; the R form did not.
lines.but: Only ten people took part, and everyone could tell when they had been given a drug.
how: Ten healthy people had the S form, the R form and a dummy, a month apart.
On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self.
On the R form, the same people described relaxation, and their brain scans moved the other way.
The ordinary mix of the two forms was never given to these same ten people.

cards.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.

questions: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?

lines.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year, and answered, said they'd sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.

cards.statement: In one big survey, people sought emergency treatment more often after LSD than after magic mushrooms.

questions: How is MDA different from MDMA?

lines.short: It seemed to last longer, with more visuals and less anxiety: at 6 hours MDA was still clearly felt and MDMA wasn't. That's one small lab study.
lines.but: MDA and MDMA weren't tested on the same people. The MDMA results, from other people in earlier studies, stop at 6 hours.
how: 12 healthy adults who had used MDA, or MDMA and LSD-type drugs, took MDA and a dummy pill in hospital, not told which. Their results were set beside earlier MDMA results from other people.
MDA was rated higher than MDMA for visions and 'spiritual' feelings, and lower for anxiety and loss of control. Both made people feel close to others.
Heart rate rose about 20 beats a minute after MDA and 31 after MDMA, though the paper calls them similar. Top blood pressure rose about 30 points with both.
The paper calls MDA well tolerated, but doesn't report the side effects it checked for. Why MDMA is more popular wasn't studied.

cards.statement: In a lab study, MDA brought more visions than MDMA, but less anxiety.

questions: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different?

lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 lab volunteers rated the trips alike on most measures.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.
The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more. LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints like headaches; nobody had a serious problem.
By the study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

cards.statement: Most people can't tell LSD from psilocybin if not told which they got.
In a lab test, people rated LSD and psilocybin trips much alike.

questions: What happens when meth and alcohol are taken together?
Meth with alcohol: what changes?

lines.short: With alcohol, meth raises the heart rate more and makes people feel less drunk.
lines.but: One study of nine men, with small oral doses in a laboratory.
how: Together they raised heart rate and good feelings more than either drug alone.
People felt less drunk and did better on attention tests, at the same breath alcohol.
By the third dose, a day and a half later, those extra effects were smaller.
Whether feeling less drunk leads people to drink more was not tested.

questions: Opioids with benzodiazepines: how much riskier?

lines.short: People on prescribed opioids and benzos had more overdoses than people on opioids alone.
lines.but: The studies could not separate the benzos from the reasons people were given them.
how: Among US veterans on opioid painkillers, about 3 in 1,000 died of overdose each year while also prescribed benzos.
Without a benzo prescription, under 1 in 1,000 died each year. Higher prescribed benzo doses went with more deaths.
In insured US adults, hospital visits for opioid overdose were about twice as common with both prescriptions.
Risk was also higher after the benzo prescription stopped, so something about the people may explain part of it.

cards.statement: People prescribed both opioids and benzos (calming medicines) had more overdoses than people on opioids alone.

questions: How many opioid deaths also involve alcohol?

lines.short: Alcohol was listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
lines.but: Alcohol is often left off death records, and these counts do not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008.
Alcohol was listed more often in men's deaths (17 in 100) than in women's (about 10 in 100).
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged alcohol involved in about 12 in 100 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Without knowing how many people drink with opioids, these counts cannot say how much alcohol adds to risk. Two reviews describe no study in people that measured it.

cards.statement: Alcohol is listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.

questions: What is serotonin syndrome, and how do doctors spot it?

lines.short: Doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking, sweating and restlessness when serotonin may be too high.
lines.but: The checklist was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses, against that unit's own diagnosis.
how: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) is too much serotonin activity, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. It ranges from mild to severe.
Doctors examine the person for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.
In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs matched the unit's diagnosis in about 84 of 100 people diagnosed. An older checklist matched about 75 of 100.
Everyone had taken an overdose, and mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects. No independent test of the checklist was found.

cards.statement: Mild signs of serotonin syndrome (too much serotonin activity) can look like ordinary drug effects.
Mild serotonin syndrome is easy to tell apart from ordinary drug effects.

questions: What happens when cocaine and alcohol are used together?
Cocaine with alcohol: what happens to the heart?

lines.short: Together they make a new substance, cocaethylene, and hearts beat faster than with cocaine alone.
lines.but: Small hospital studies of 8 and 6 people. None measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.
how: Eight adults who already used both drugs took cocaine by the nose on a hospital ward. With alcohol, their heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute, against 74 with cocaine alone.
There was also about 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in their blood, and cocaethylene, which the body makes only when both drugs are there and which leaves the blood more slowly than cocaine.

In a second study, cocaine went into a vein with alcohol. Cocaethylene formed again, but stayed at a small fraction of the cocaine level, and none of it appeared when cocaine was given without alcohol.

Cocaethylene has been found in people's blood after both drugs, including after deaths, but such tests cannot show what caused a death. In over 1,000 emergency-room tests, people positive for both drugs had no more heart problems than people positive for one.

cards.statement: When people use cocaine with alcohol, the body makes a new substance, cocaethylene, that forms only when both are there.
Cocaine with alcohol makes the heart beat faster than cocaine alone.

questions: Can cocaine make someone feel less drunk?
Does cocaine hide how drunk someone is?

lines.short: People given cocaine with alcohol did not feel more drunk, and sometimes slightly less.
lines.but: This is second-hand from one review of small studies, and no one tested driving.
how: A review gathered 14 small laboratory studies. The four that asked how drunk people felt had 8 to 11 people each. Those studies have not been read here, so the figures are second-hand.
In three of the four, people said they felt a little less drunk with cocaine; in one, nothing changed. Two of the three falls were too small to be clear.
Cocaine also made some alcohol-affected test scores less poor, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about 10 percent lower.

Nobody asked other people how drunk someone looked, and no study tested driving. Of drivers who died in crashes, about 4 in 100 had both drugs in their blood, so the mix did not protect them from alcohol's effects.

questions: Cannabis with alcohol: is driving worse than with either alone?

lines.short: Cannabis with alcohol was linked to worse driving, about the sum of each.
lines.but: Neither study measures crash risk or impairment on a road.
how: In a driving simulator, 18 healthy adults had a usual lane weave of about 31 cm. A model of their driving gave a rise of 1.3 cm with cannabis (THC 5 µg/L in blood), 2.1 cm with alcohol (breath 0.05) and 3.4 cm with both.

In US records of drivers in fatal crashes who had a blood test, a model for a man aged 45 gave 64 in 100 with a recorded unsafe driving action at a blood alcohol of 0.05, and 66 in 100 if cannabis was also found. At 0.08 it was 70 and 71 in 100.
Both studies fit the two effects adding up, not clearly more. Other studies disagree on this.
A simulator is not a road, and a positive cannabis test shows it was in the blood, not that someone was impaired. Neither study asked how impaired drivers felt.

cards.statement: In a driving simulator, cannabis and alcohol together made lane weaving worse than either one alone.

questions: GHB or GBL with alcohol: what changes?

lines.short: People who took GHB with alcohol were less awake more often at hospital.
lines.but: Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts were not known.
how: In 609 emergency patients who took GHB or GBL, 59 in 100 of those who also had alcohol were less awake, against 49 in 100 of those who did not. People who took other drugs were left out. Less awake means a Glasgow Coma Score under 13.
Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Across all patients, that is about 20 and 8 in 100.

Slow breathing (8 in 100 with alcohol, 12 without), breathing tubes (6 in 100 with alcohol, 4 without) and discharge did not clearly differ, but the study could not rule out a difference. Two people died, both with alcohol.
In 16 healthy volunteers, blood oxygen fell 2.1 points with both drugs, more than with either alone. That is a different measure from the patient study.

cards.statement: Among emergency patients who'd taken GHB or GBL, those who'd also had alcohol more often went to critical care.

questions: Does mixing caffeine with alcohol change my hangover?

lines.short: People who drank beer with added caffeine had about the same hangover as those without caffeine.
lines.but: The study was small and did not test energy drinks.
how: 64 young adults drank beer in a lab, and chance decided who got caffeine added.
Everyone slept in the lab and rated their hangover and sleep in the morning.

questions: Does naltrexone help people drink less?

lines.short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.
lines.but: Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.
how: Naltrexone is a tablet. Dozens of trials gave it or dummy pills, mostly for 3 months, usually with counselling as well.
About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely.
People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common.
When compared directly, naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same, but most people in that comparison were in one trial.

cards.statement: Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely.
Fewer people went back to heavy drinking on naltrexone than on dummy pills.

questions: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter?

lines.short: Common among people who use illegal drugs. It makes one drug's effects hard to study.
lines.but: The numbers come second-hand from reviews. They vary a lot between groups and studies.
how: In ecstasy studies, 90 to 100 in 100 people also used cannabis. So a study of ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once.
At underground raves, up to 75 in 100 people used several drugs, five on average at the last rave.
In most of 23 studies of teens, the biggest group used little or nothing. But every study found a group that used several. Most often it was alcohol, tobacco and cannabis: 6 to 29 in 100 teens.
Studies that sort adults into groups by the drugs they use found 2 to 8 groups. Bigger studies, and ones that asked about more drugs, found more. So what they find depends partly on how they look.

cards.statement: In studies of ecstasy, almost everyone also used cannabis.

questions: What happens when you mix MDMA with alcohol?

lines.short: People felt just as drunk as on alcohol alone, but less sleepy, and test scores fell about as far. Blood MDMA peaked 13% higher, in a lab study of 9 men.
lines.but: Only 9 men, in a lab. Heart measurements were taken but never reported.
how: 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four lab sessions, a week apart. They got MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they wouldn't know which.
With both, the sleepy feeling from alcohol went away. Feeling drunk didn't: if anything, it was rated a bit higher, though not clearly.
On a timed symbol test, scores at their worst fell about as much as with alcohol alone, but for about 1 hour, not 2 to 3. Only with both was reaction time clearly slower than with the dummy.

Blood MDMA peaked 13% higher and blood alcohol 15% lower; the authors call these small changes. Nobody rated how well they thought they did, though they felt more energetic and efficient than with alcohol alone. Nobody drove.

cards.statement: Taking MDMA with alcohol makes you feel less drunk.
With MDMA, blood alcohol was a bit lower, yet people felt just as drunk.

questions: What if I take LSD and MDMA at the same time?

lines.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
lines.but: Healthy people took one amount of each, in a calm hospital room. Nothing serious happened, but 24 people can't show rare dangers.
how: 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which.

With both, top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone; heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was not clearly higher than on LSD alone.
Bad-feeling, fear and complaint scores were not clearly lower than on LSD alone. Nobody had a serious problem. On nausea, the paper contradicts itself.
The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later.

cards.statement: Taking MDMA with LSD pushes heart rate and blood pressure higher than LSD alone.
Adding MDMA to LSD has been shown to make a bad trip less likely.

questions: What does one dose of meth do to the body and mood?

lines.short: One snorted dose raises heart rate and blood pressure and makes people feel high.
lines.but: These were single lab doses in people used to meth, not binges. One lab only.
how: In lab studies, one snorted dose raised heart rate and blood pressure.
People felt good, high and stimulated, more with bigger doses.
They also felt more jittery and sweaty, mostly at the largest dose.
These were single doses in people used to meth, all from one lab.

questions: What does a meth overdose look like?

lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.

cards.statement: Meth poisoning can make the body get very hot.
A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart and fast breathing.

questions: Why do some people overheat on MDMA?

lines.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
lines.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies. They couldn't tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees. But the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses. In another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.

cards.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.

questions: Can drinking lots of water on MDMA lead to low blood salt?

lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill. So they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.

The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water. In one study, 8 healthy men given one MDMA capsule had a rise in the water-holding hormone, and their blood salt fell a little, not to a low level. It had no proper comparison, and a study of 32 people found no clear rise in a related marker.

cards.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.

questions: What does MDMA feel like?

lines.short: Mostly good: in lab studies, 67 in 100 called it positive afterwards. It lasted about four hours. Many also got a dry mouth or a clenched jaw.
lines.but: These were healthy volunteers in a lab, given a known pill and nothing else.
how: In Basel labs, 136 healthy adults rated the good feeling about 80 out of 100, against 3 or 4 on a dummy pill. In a study of 32, people felt more open and closer to others.
Unwanted effects came too: 55 in 100 had a dry mouth and 40 in 100 of those asked clenched their jaw. Looking back, 67 in 100 called it positive, 15 in 100 disappointing or bad.
It began in about half an hour on average and lasted about four hours. For some the start was slow; an antidepressant given first cut the effect. Nobody took more, so that wasn't tested.
At a London club, people who took ecstasy weren't clearly happier than other clubbers. Two days later they felt sadder, but not a week later. Pills were untested, so MDMA's part is unclear.

cards.statement: In a club study, people who took ecstasy felt sadder and less sociable two days later than other clubbers.
In lab studies, 15 in 100 people later called their MDMA experience disappointing or bad.

questions: What does ketamine do to perception, thinking and the sense of self while it is working?
What does ketamine do to perception, thinking and sense of self?

lines.short: Compared with a salt-water day, people felt cut off from themselves and their thinking got muddled.
lines.but: Raters could probably tell who had ketamine, and the studies disagree a lot about how big the effects are.
how: Healthy volunteers were given ketamine into a vein and, to compare, salt water, with the same ratings both times. One study had no salt-water day: it compared people with themselves before the drug.

On the ketamine day, scores for psychosis-like experiences, for feeling cut off, and for odd perceptions were much higher. Pooling 36 such studies in 725 volunteers gives the same answer, from the strongest moment of each study.
People became suspicious and their thinking became muddled. What was scored as hallucinations was mostly real sights and sounds that seemed changed, not seeing things that were not there.

Two studies rated people again after the drip stopped, and scores were back to their usual level within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour. The 36 pooled studies measured nothing after the session, so they say nothing about how long it lasts.

cards.statement: In ketamine lab studies, hallucinations mostly meant seeing things that were not there.

questions: How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?

lines.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

cards.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.

questions: How does THC move through the body after smoking and after eating, and how long does it stay in blood and urine?
How fast does THC rise and fall in the blood, smoked or eaten?

lines.short: Smoked, THC peaks in the blood within minutes; eaten, it rises slowly over hours.
lines.but: Old, small lab studies of weak cannabis, described in one review.
how: After smoking, THC in the blood peaked within minutes and fell to low levels within 2 hours.
After eating, it peaked 1 to 6 hours later, at lower levels, and the effects started later and lasted longer.
THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it can be found for days to weeks.

After one cigarette the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and cannabis was found for 67 and 93 days in two people who used heavily; a positive test does not show when or how much.

questions: Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?

lines.short: It may. Feeling calm, open and ready beforehand went with easier trips, and feeling anxious went with more anxiety during the trip.
lines.but: These are links: no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.
how: About 650 people planning their own trip answered surveys; about 200 answered enough to be counted. Those who felt calm, open and ready the day before said the trip was less hard.
In lab studies of LSD, feeling anxious before the dose went with more anxiety. A better mood beforehand went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones.
Bigger links come from people looking back on how they'd felt, asked at the same time as how the trip went, so they don't show what came first.
Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice. But a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.

cards.statement: In surveys, people who felt calm, open and ready the day before a psychedelic trip said it was less hard.

questions: Do the place and the people around me affect a psychedelic trip?

lines.short: Maybe a little. In surveys, people who felt safe and supported reported slightly fewer hard moments.
lines.but: People rated this looking back, and the one study that asked beforehand found only a weak link.
how: In a study that asked the day before, feeling good about the place and people went with slightly easier trips. But the link was weak and could be chance.
Almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca answered a survey. Those who felt safer and better supported at the ceremony reported a little less fear.
In a US survey, people who blamed a lack of support for their hardest trip said it was harder than people who did not.

No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, to compare them. A review of 25 trials found none either; some used plain hospital rooms, others disguised them as living rooms.

cards.statement: In surveys, feeling safe and supported on a psychedelic trip went with far fewer difficult moments.

questions: Is using ketamine linked to bladder problems?

lines.short: Ketamine is linked to bladder problems seen in over 4,000 patients. In one survey, about 1 in 4 people who used it blamed it for urine problems.
lines.but: No study compared how often people who use ketamine and people who don't get these problems. So none can show ketamine caused them.
how: In over 4,000 patients seen by doctors, mostly in Asia, about 77 in 100 needed to pee often and 60 in 100 had bladder pain.
In about 3 in 10 of these patients, urine had backed up and swollen a kidney. About 8 in 100 had weaker kidney function.
The survey was online, mostly in the UK: 1,285 people who had used ketamine in the past year. Those who used more reported more symptoms.
Of 251 people who described how symptoms changed, 128 said they eased after stopping. No study compared people who stopped with those who kept using.

cards.statement: In one survey of people who used ketamine, about 1 in 4 blamed it for urine problems.
Bladder problems linked to ketamine never ease, even after people stop using it.

questions: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?

lines.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported anxiety or panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.

cards.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.

questions: What do people say they meet on DMT?

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

cards.statement: Only people on DMT describe meeting a kind being that gives them a message.
Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.

questions: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?

lines.short: Maybe a little. People who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled a bit less fear. They also reported fewer problems later.
lines.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear. Church hymns or sermons went with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.

cards.statement: In a survey of almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, fasting went with less fear or fewer later problems.
The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.

questions: Does music change how a trip goes?

lines.short: Nobody knows for sure: no study we read compared music with silence. 18 of 19 patients said music helped at times; 10 said it sometimes made things harder.
lines.but: The one test that compared two playlists had just 10 people, so it could easily miss a difference.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.

Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time, so feeling better may have made them describe the music more warmly.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest trip to music they disliked didn't rate that trip as harder than others did.

cards.statement: In one psilocybin clinic study, about half of 19 patients said the music sometimes made things harder.

questions: Does music change how a ketamine treatment session goes?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
lines.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.

cards.statement: Music has been shown to make ketamine treatment for depression work better.

questions: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

cards.statement: In a lab psilocybin study, fewer than 1 in 20 volunteers felt strong fear.
In a Johns Hopkins psilocybin study, fewer than 5 in 100 volunteers felt strong fear.
Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single psilocybin session among their 5 most meaningful experiences.

questions: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?

lines.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
lines.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.

cards.statement: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences.
Ketamine trip reports read more like near-death accounts than those for any other drug.

questions: Do trips show you the truth, or just change your beliefs?

lines.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But after a retreat, beliefs shifted a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
lines.but: The main study had no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people who said a trip had changed their beliefs to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

cards.statement: People whose beliefs change after a trip start to believe in bad luck too.
Beliefs can shift after a psychedelic retreat and still be shifted 6 months on.

questions: Can drug levels change after death?

lines.short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall after death and differ between blood vessels, so a drug can look more or less involved in a death than it was.
lines.but: Nobody knows how often, or by how much, levels change in an ordinary death.
how: In four suspected overdose deaths picked as examples, a drug's level could be 3.5 to 6.6 times higher in one blood vessel than another in the same body. A hospital medicine varied only 1.6 times.
In one person, all imipramine samples after death were about 2 to 8 times the earlier hospital level.
A collection of 5,375 cases from published reports and Finnish lab records found that the gap between samples from different body parts varied more than tenfold between drugs.
In bodies tested more than once, levels of about a dozen drugs rose, including fentanyl and methadone; others, like THC, fell. First samples came about 17 hours after death on average.

cards.statement: Once a person has died, the level of a drug in their blood no longer changes.

questions: Did teen cannabis use rise after US states legalised it?

lines.short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.
lines.but: Just 7 states had surveys from both before and after the change, and only for its first few years.
how: Surveys gathered 1.4 million answers from US high school students, 1993 to 2017. Each state was compared before and after its law, against other states.
After recreational laws, the odds of past-month cannabis use were 8% lower. That is not 8 fewer teens in 100, but at most about 2.
Laws for medical cannabis, in 27 states and Washington, DC, were not linked to teen use either way, once other things were counted.
The authors suggest shops that check age make cannabis harder for teens to get. Their source: a 2012 news article. The study didn't test it.

cards.statement: Teen cannabis use went up after US states made recreational cannabis legal.

questions: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?

lines.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
lines.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them. This was done 3 times, each time with 6 new people sitting in: 18 in all.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once on at least one of 4 tests. A lab check would have confirmed it for 3 to 7, depending on the test.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.

cards.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.

questions: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?

lines.short: Yes, it can. In one study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine in their urine above the sports limit of the time.
lines.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, which had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.

cards.statement: Eating poppy seeds can make you fail a sports drug test.

questions: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

cards.statement: After Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use as a crime in 2001, drug use fell.

questions: Do police and sniffer dogs at festivals stop people taking drugs?

lines.short: Not by much, going by what people said. With sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 said they'd still use drugs, against 77 with no police, in an Australian online survey.
lines.but: It's what people said they'd do at a made-up festival, not what they really did.
how: 2,115 Australian festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, volunteered for an online survey. Each read about a made-up festival with no police, and one with police, riot police, sniffer dogs or police working with health services.
With any police, 70 in 100 said they'd use drugs and 53 in 100 that they'd carry drugs in, against 77 and 63 with no police. With sniffer dogs, 47 in 100 said they'd carry drugs in.
Slightly more said they'd buy drugs inside the festival when police were there: 40 against 37 in 100. The authors worry those drugs may not be what they're sold as, which wasn't checked.
Police working with health services made almost no difference: 75 in 100 still said they'd use drugs. The study says nothing about how much people would take.

cards.statement: In a survey, most festival-goers said sniffer dogs would stop them using drugs.

questions: What side effects does MDMA cause in therapy trials?

lines.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
lines.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.

cards.statement: MDMA therapy papers left out side effects that their own trial records listed.

questions: Do some people feel MDMA more strongly than others?

lines.short: Yes. The biggest link was the amount per kilo of body weight. Given the same amount, lighter people got more per kilo, which went with stronger effects.
lines.but: That's one lab, with healthy volunteers in a hospital, most of them trying MDMA for the first time.
how: 194 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 took MDMA in hospital, one set amount each time. On another day they took a dummy pill.
The amount per kilo of body weight went most with how strong it felt. Women and men didn't clearly differ once weight was counted, though an earlier report suggested women may feel more bad effects.

People who tend to worry, or who felt anxious and low just before, said they felt more anxious than calmer people did. People more open to new things felt closer to others. None of these links was strong.
Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

cards.statement: In lab studies, people who felt anxious and low just before MDMA felt more anxious than calm people did.

questions: Does MDMA-assisted therapy help PTSD more than therapy with a dummy pill?

lines.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused talking therapy.

cards.statement: In MDMA trials for PTSD, many people given a dummy pill plus therapy also no longer had PTSD.

questions: Did the US regulator approve MDMA therapy for PTSD in 2024?

lines.short: No. The US regulator turned it down in August 2024, after its expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show it works.
lines.but: We read the panel's notes, but we only know the decision second-hand.
how: In June 2024, the regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show the treatment works, and 10 to 1 that the benefits didn't outweigh the risks.
Panel members worried that people could tell which pill they'd had. In one trial, 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right.
They also doubted the later check of whether benefits lasted, and noted that no study separated the drug's effect from the therapy's.
The regulator's own staff said the main trials had no lab tests on treatment days, and the company didn't log euphoria as a side effect, so misuse risk was harder to judge.

cards.statement: In 2024 the US regulator approved MDMA therapy for PTSD.

questions: Do the MDMA therapy trials hold up?

lines.short: It's not settled. Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but can't show how much was the drug itself, or for how long.
lines.but: One sponsor ran both trials, and in the one that asked, most people knew their pill.
how: Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA and therapy than with a dummy pill and the same therapy. Neither tested MDMA against usual talking therapy.
But in the second trial most people could tell which pill they had, and neither trial reports measuring what they expected.
The company says a later visit showed the benefit lasted. The regulator said it wasn't built to show that: about 3 in 10 didn't come, some knew their pill, and some had other treatment in between.
In 2024 the US regulator said no, after its advisers voted 9 to 2 that it wasn't shown to work. Three papers on earlier trials were withdrawn for not disclosing rule-breaking at one site.

cards.statement: MDMA therapy for PTSD has been shown to work better than usual talking therapy.
A journal withdrew three earlier MDMA therapy studies over rule-breaking at one trial site.

questions: Does MDMA therapy ease anxiety in people with a serious illness?

lines.short: In one small trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.
lines.but: The difference could be chance: only 18 people took part, and most could tell which pill they had.
how: 18 adults with anxiety about cancer or another serious illness took part. They had two long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
A month later, anxiety scores had dropped about 24 points with MDMA. They dropped 9 points with the dummy pill. The scale runs from 20 to 80.
With so few people, the true difference could be anywhere from none to very large.
Later everyone got MDMA. Scores stayed lower a year later, but there was no group left to compare.

questions: Does MDMA therapy help social anxiety in autistic adults?

lines.short: In one small trial, social anxiety eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.
lines.but: Only 12 autistic adults took part, and almost all could tell which pill they got.
how: 12 autistic adults with strong social anxiety took part. They had two long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
A month later, social anxiety scores had dropped about 44 points with MDMA and 19 with the dummy pill.
People guessed their pill right in 22 of 23 sessions, so what they expected may have shaped what they reported.
With so few people, the true benefit could be small or large.

questions: Can MDMA therapy help with anything besides PTSD?

lines.short: Nobody can say yet. Outside PTSD, it's been tried for a few things. They include tinnitus, drinking problems, and anxiety in autistic adults or in people who are very ill.
lines.but: Each had one tiny trial at most, the biggest with 18 people.
how: Reviews up to 2024 found one trial each. There were 18 people anxious about a serious illness, 12 autistic adults with social anxiety, and 13 people with tinnitus.
A study of 14 people with alcohol problems, and one of 6 couples, had no comparison group.
In the serious-illness trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but the trial was too small to be sure.
A critical review found only the two later PTSD trials were randomized with over 15 people per group. It called even those results a signal needing repeating.

cards.statement: MDMA therapy has even been tried, in a small trial, for ringing in the ears (tinnitus).

questions: Is ketamine as good as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for hard-to-treat depression?

lines.short: Two big trials disagree: a US trial found ketamine drips at least as good as ECT. But in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.
lines.but: Everyone knew whether they got ketamine or ECT, and the trials took different people, so nobody knows why they disagree.
how: In a US trial of 403 adults, mostly outpatients without psychosis, 55 in 100 on ketamine drips said their depression halved, against 41 on ECT.
In a Swedish trial of 186 hospital patients, some with psychosis, 63 in 100 got well after ECT, against 46 after ketamine.
A review combining hospital trials also found ECT eased depression more than ketamine, but about half its data came from that Swedish trial.
In Sweden, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.

cards.statement: In a big US trial, ketamine drips eased depression at least as much as ECT.
Two big trials comparing ketamine drips with ECT for depression came to the same answer.
Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.

questions: What side effects do people have from ketamine treatment for depression?

lines.short: With ketamine for depression, studies most often found headache and dizziness. Next came feeling unreal and higher blood pressure. Most soon passed.
lines.but: Only 12 of 60 studies checked again 2 weeks or more after the last dose, and just 5 checked the bladder.
how: A review of 60 studies up to 2016 listed side effects but could not say how often each happens. Most people had a single dose.
Raised blood pressure and heart rate came during or just after the drip and mostly settled within 90 minutes.
In a 7-person trial, all felt 'high' on ketamine and none on salt water. On average it was gone within 2 hours after the drip.
In a large trial, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect within 3 weeks, against 32 in 100 on ECT.

cards.statement: Most of 60 studies of ketamine for depression checked the bladder.
In a big trial, ketamine treatment for depression caused more moderate or severe side effects than ECT.

questions: Does a CBD medicine reduce seizures in a severe childhood epilepsy?

lines.short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.
lines.but: The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result did not always hold up.
how: First trial, 120 children: seizures at least halved in 43 in 100 on CBD and 27 on the dummy liquid. That gap could be chance.
Second trial, 198 children: 44 and 49 in 100 in two CBD groups saw seizures at least halve. On the dummy liquid, 26 did.
The second report said backup checks agreed. Yet with missing diary days filled in, one CBD group no longer clearly beat the dummy liquid.
On CBD, 23 to 36 in 100 children were sleepy, against 10 to 14 on the dummy liquid. Shop CBD was not tested.

cards.statement: Trials show that CBD oil from a shop cuts seizures in children with a severe epilepsy.
In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in children with Dravet syndrome, a form of epilepsy.

questions: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?

lines.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
lines.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.
how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it harder to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after ketamine. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.

cards.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.

questions: Does psilocybin help depression?

lines.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
lines.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.

cards.statement: In a US trial, one psilocybin session with therapists lowered depression scores more than a vitamin pill did.
In a US trial, people got one psilocybin session or a vitamin pill. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin.
In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.

questions: Is psilocybin better than a standard antidepressant for depression?

lines.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
lines.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.

cards.statement: In a trial of 59 people, psilocybin clearly beat the antidepressant escitalopram on the main depression score.
Six months after a trial, the psilocybin group was clearly less depressed than the group on the antidepressant escitalopram.

questions: Can psilocybin help people drink less?

lines.short: Maybe. In one trial, people given psilocybin with talk therapy drank heavily on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 with a comparison pill.
lines.but: Almost everyone could tell if they got psilocybin, and people reported their own drinking.
how: At 2 US universities, 93 adults dependent on alcohol were offered 12 talk-therapy sessions. Chance decided who also got psilocybin twice or a comparison pill.
Heavy drinking had already more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of therapy. That was before any psilocybin or comparison pill.
After about 94 in 100 sessions, people guessed right whether they had psilocybin. So what they expected may explain part of the gap.

cards.statement: In a psilocybin trial for drinking problems, heavy drinking more than halved before anyone was given psilocybin.

questions: Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?

lines.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.

cards.statement: Psilocybin has been shown to help people quit smoking.

questions: Does microdosing magic mushrooms do anything, or is it placebo?

lines.short: In two trials, people could feel a magic mushroom or LSD microdose on the day. But their mood and thinking were not clearly better than with a dummy capsule.
lines.but: Only a small one-week trial used just magic mushrooms; the bigger one was mostly LSD, and neither lasted months.
how: In Argentina, 34 people took magic mushroom capsules one week and look-alike capsules of an ordinary mushroom another. Mood and creativity did not improve.
A bigger study: 240 people mixed their own microdoses, mostly LSD, with empty capsules. After 4 weeks, the dummy group was not clearly worse off.
People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.
Everyone in both studies took capsules, so neither can show it is all placebo. People might have got better anyway.

cards.statement: In a trial with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms made people more creative.
In trials with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms or LSD made people's mood better than the dummies did.
People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.

questions: Does esketamine nasal spray work for hard-to-treat depression?

lines.short: In two big trials, esketamine spray (a form of ketamine) did a little better than a dummy spray. Only one trial passed its main test.
lines.but: About 1 in 4 felt detached or unreal on esketamine, so many may have known which spray they got, and nobody asked.
how: In two trials, adults whose depression had not lifted on two antidepressants got esketamine or a dummy spray. All started a new antidepressant.
After 4 weeks, depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine. A fast start was not shown.
Among people whose depression had lifted, 45 in 100 switched to a dummy spray relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine.
The company behind it paid for every trial. Two critics argue relapses may partly be effects of stopping; the trial could not tell.

cards.statement: Esketamine nasal spray passed its main test in both of its big 4-week trials.
People whose depression lifted on esketamine relapsed more often when switched to a dummy spray.

questions: What does MDMA do to sex drive, erections and orgasm?

lines.short: People say desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
lines.but: It's 35 people who chose to talk about it, remembering past experiences. Nobody tested their pills.
how: In Israel, 20 men and 15 women who had used MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex. All 35 said desire went up, and 32 said they were more satisfied.
Of the 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker and 8 stronger. 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women said orgasm took longer, and 3 people said they couldn't reach it but were still more satisfied.
In Northern Ireland, 98 people were interviewed. A little over half said MDMA was more about closeness than sex. Some men said they couldn't get an erection; others described strong desire.
Some described one-night stands and regret. Condoms were rare on ecstasy, but also rare without drugs, so the study can't show MDMA made sex riskier.

cards.statement: Most men get harder erections on MDMA.
In one survey, most men who had used MDMA before sex said orgasm took longer.

questions: How do people feel in the days and weeks after a psychedelic?

lines.short: Often better than before: less low mood and stress, more wellbeing, in most studies that checked. Some people got headaches, usually for a day or two, or slept badly.
lines.but: Most studies had no blind dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause, and most were supported sessions, not recreational use.
how: A review gathered 48 studies of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, with 1,774 people in all. People answered the same questionnaires before, and again a day to a month after.
Most studies that checked (70 to 90 in 100) found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, mindfulness and closeness to others. None found mental health worse on average.
Of 25 studies that said they looked for problems, 14 found some: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then poor sleep, tension and exhaustion.
One person had severe anxiety, and one went back to using methamphetamine. Half the studies didn't say whether they looked for problems at all.

cards.statement: In studies that looked for problems after psychedelics like psilocybin or LSD, severe anxiety was the most common.

questions: Can psilocybin change your personality?

lines.short: Not proven. After psilocybin, people rated themselves about 3 to 5 points more 'open' 1 to 3 months later, on a scale where the average adult scores 50.
lines.but: These were people rating themselves before and after, and no study checked that against how they acted. The one test against another drug found no difference.
how: 52 healthy volunteers, new to psychedelics and mostly religious or spiritual, rated themselves 2.8 points more open 1 to 2 months after their psilocybin session. Their other four traits didn't clearly change.

The rise came from the 30 who had a full mystical experience, and about a third of all the volunteers scored lower afterwards. Over a year later, that group was still about 4 points up, a result right on the edge of chance.
Most of them came from one trial. There, 15 people who got psilocybin first and 15 who got a stimulant first scored no differently on personality 2 months later.

In 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression, openness rose 4.9 points by 3 months, and they rated themselves less anxious and more sociable. The researchers say mood may explain those last two changes.

cards.statement: In a lab study, about a third of people rated themselves less 'open' after psilocybin.
It's been shown that psilocybin can change your personality.

questions: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?

lines.short: Because tolerance may drop during a break, reviews say. In one study, 3 people died of an overdose after a hospital detox. All 3 had stayed for the whole programme.
lines.but: Nobody measured anyone's tolerance. And it's 3 deaths in one small study.
how: 137 people were followed for a year after a 28-day hospital detox in London. All 3 overdose deaths came within 4 months, among the 37 who finished both the detox and the programme. None of the 100 who left earlier died that way.

The researchers read this as lost tolerance but never measured it. The people who died also differed in other ways: 4 of the 5 who died from any cause had lived alone, against 16 in 100 of the others.
Two reviews offer the same idea but give no numbers: not how long a break must be, how fast tolerance falls, or how much the risk rises. The main study behind them looked at hair samples.
One review describes two studies of people on methadone. Their tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

cards.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
In one study, people who stayed to the end of a detox programme had fewer overdose deaths later.

questions: How common is using drugs alone, and why do people do it?

lines.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites said they'd used alone at least once in the past week. The most-picked reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
lines.but: It's one survey in one part of Canada, of people who already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, answered a survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

cards.statement: In British Columbia in 2016 and 2017, about 7 in 10 people who died of a drug overdose were using alone.
Few people who go to harm reduction sites use drugs alone.

questions: What level of MDMA in blood is fatal?

lines.short: These studies do not establish a fatal cutoff; the measured levels overlap.
lines.but: The groups are small, and some London table decimals are unclear in the scan.
how: In Sheffield, England (1992–2008), levels in deaths attributed to MDMA overlapped levels in injury deaths. The middle value was about 7 times the injury-group value, but was not a cutoff.
The London table values overlap if unclear decimal points have been read correctly. Its survivors included severely ill people, not healthy people after ordinary use.
A Finnish table’s 0% concerns poisoning with MDMA as the main finding, not every possible contribution. It records what certifiers decided.
Sampling time and specimen matter. The London tables do not say when every sample was taken. No study here gives a healthy ordinary-use comparison.

questions: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?

lines.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
lines.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.

cards.statement: In one large study, most alcohol or drug poisoning deaths after leaving prison came in the first 4 weeks.
The risk of dying is highest in the first week after leaving prison.

questions: How much more likely are people with problem cocaine use to die?

lines.short: Each year, 5 to 62 in 1,000 died: 4 to 8 times others their age.
lines.but: All groups injected, smoked crack daily, were in treatment or arrested; none only snorted.
how: Seven groups in six countries were studied between 1985 and 2005. Each year, between about 5 and 62 in 1,000 died.
Four groups were compared with people of the same age and sex: 4 to 8 times as many died.
Among people who injected, AIDS and overdose were the main causes. In a crack treatment group in Brazil, it was gunshot wounds and AIDS.
Many also used heroin or had HIV, and only age and sex were taken into account. So this does not show what cocaine itself does.

cards.statement: In four groups who used cocaine, 4 to 8 times as many died as others of the same age and sex.

questions: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?

lines.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.
lines.but: Surviving doesn't prove naloxone saved a life, since most overdoses aren't fatal, and only one study compared death rates.
