how: In 19 Massachusetts towns, 2006 to 2009, 2,912 people who might see an opioid overdose got training and nasal naloxone. They reported 327 rescue attempts.
Where more than 1 in 1,000 people were trained, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower, and nearly half lower after allowing for other differences.
Every town had the programme by 2008, so the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones. It never printed how many people died.
Across 17 studies, trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, mostly for heroin overdoses; 20 are known to have died. Since most overdoses aren't fatal, lives saved are unknown.

cards.statement: When 96 in 100 people given naloxone for an opioid overdose survive, naloxone saved 96 lives in 100.

questions: Would I know if someone was overdosing on opioids?

lines.short: Not always. On a written test, people trained by overdose programmes spotted about 7 of 9 opioid overdoses. People without that training spotted about 5 of 9.
lines.but: It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked, not real overdoses. Nobody was tested before training, so training may not be the reason.
how: In 2005 and 2006, 62 people at six US overdose programmes read 16 short stories. Each was based on what someone who injects drugs had called an overdose. Medical experts had decided 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone, and 7 were not.
Trained people spotted about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, untrained people about 5. Trained people still didn't choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9; untrained people missed about 3.
Both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 stories right. Even the experts said there wasn't enough information in about a quarter of their answers.
The paper doesn't say which stories people got wrong. So it can't show which signs get missed, or whether people can tell a heavy nod from an overdose.

cards.statement: Even after overdose training, people missed some opioid overdoses on a written test.

questions: How can I get a family member who refuses help into treatment?

lines.short: Family skills training called CRAFT worked best in trials. In one, 64 in 100 relatives who'd refused help started treatment, against 30 with confrontation training and 13 with counselling to join Al-Anon.
lines.but: Just four small US trials, and two came from a team that includes CRAFT's developer.
how: The biggest trial had 130 family members, mostly women, living with someone with a drinking problem. Each got one of three approaches by chance. Families with recent or severe violence were left out.

Within 6 months, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment after CRAFT. It was 30 after training for a family confrontation, and 13 after counselling to join Al-Anon. Seven in 10 families chose not to hold the confrontation.
Across four trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, 67 in 100 relatives started treatment with CRAFT, against 18 in 100 with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches: about 3 times as often.

In the biggest trial, family members felt less depressed and angry after 6 months in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment. Every group got some help, so no approach can take the credit.

cards.statement: Confronting someone as a family works best to get them into treatment.
Family members only feel better if their loved one starts treatment.

questions: How common are bad trips, and can problems last?

lines.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
lines.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 said they'd thought of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.

57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But people who hadn't used them weren't asked, so it's unknown how many would have had these anyway.

cards.statement: Bad trips are fairly common among people who've used psychedelics.

questions: Is 'excited delirium' a real cause of death?

lines.short: The label alone does not establish what caused a death.
lines.but: The cases were selected for reports. They cannot give the risk per encounter.
how: The reviews describe extreme agitation, but no validated definition or specific autopsy sign. The label is also used with living people.
In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. That included sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint.
Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; 28 had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint.
Researchers disagree about restraint, drugs and the agitated state. These reports cannot tell how much each caused.

cards.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.

questions: Does LSD damage your chromosomes?

lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
lines.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.

cards.statement: Studies of people given pure LSD found clearly more broken chromosomes.
The early studies that linked LSD to broken chromosomes ruled out other drugs.
The LSD chromosome scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish.

questions: How long does meth stay in the blood?

lines.short: After the blood level peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours to fall by half.
lines.but: It differs from person to person, and it is not the same as how long the effects last.
how: It takes about 10 to 12 hours for the blood level to fall by half.
This is about the same whether meth is snorted, smoked, injected or swallowed.
People differ: from about 8 to 18 hours in one study.
How long it stays in the blood is not how long the effects last.

questions: How long does ketamine stay in the blood?

lines.short: It drops fast at first, then falls by half every two to three hours.
lines.but: The two studies had only six and three people, and timed mainly doses into a vein.
how: Blood samples after a dose into a vein show a quick fall, then a slower one.
One study found a half-life of about three hours, the other about two hours.
The body turns most ketamine into norketamine; after a swallowed dose there is far more norketamine than ketamine.
Only one rough figure is given for a swallowed dose, and none for a nose spray.

questions: How fast does cocaine act, and for how long?

lines.short: Smoked or injected, the high peaks in about a minute and fades within 30 minutes.
lines.but: Small lab studies of men who used cocaine often. Snorting was not measured.
how: Nine men who both smoked and injected cocaine stayed on a research ward. They got set doses, each given over 15 seconds.
The high, a faster heartbeat and higher blood pressure peaked after about a minute. The high was low by 15 to 30 minutes.
Cocaine stayed in the blood after the high had gone. In 4 other men, the level halved only about every 40 to 80 minutes in the later hours.
An older review says snorted cocaine peaks later, with the high at 10 to 20 minutes, and lasts longer. No study here tested what happens when people then take more.

questions: Do CBD products contain what their labels say?

lines.short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.
lines.but: One test of products bought online in 2016; products sold in shops, or today, may differ.
how: CBD is a substance from the cannabis plant. Researchers bought every CBD oil, tincture and vape liquid with a CBD label they found online.
A lab that did not know the labels tested them. 36 held more CBD than the label said, and 22 held less.
Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than a tenth, mostly holding more CBD than labelled.
No one took the products, and no urine was tested. So this can't say if they cause a high or a positive drug test.

cards.statement: CBD products usually contain what their labels say.

questions: Which harm reduction services exist for benzos, and do they work?

lines.short: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules exist. No study has shown whether they lower harm.
lines.but: The review did not judge how good the studies were, and most had no comparison group.
how: A 2025 review found 35 reports on harm reduction for benzos.

About half of the drug-checking reports tested how well testing machines find drugs. A portable machine found the designer benzo etizolam in 36 of 100 samples that had it; an infrared machine found it in 9.
At one service in Canada, people brought 139 samples they thought were Xanax. An infrared machine found alprazolam, the drug in Xanax, in 33 of them.
Studies of benzos on prescription and of stricter rules could not show what caused what. Their results were mixed.

questions: Is it dangerous to stop benzos suddenly?

lines.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
lines.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one gives no source for them.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound, and can feel like the problem the pills were for. Sleeping pills stopped after even a few nights can bring back worse sleep for a while.

Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen when cutting down slowly, and that many reports are anecdotes; the other gives no source for its warning.
The only count comes second-hand, from a 1961 study: 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

cards.statement: Benzo withdrawal can feel like the anxiety or sleep problems the pills were for.
Two expert reviews that warn of seizures after stopping benzos suddenly say how often they happen.

questions: Do meth's effects fade while it is still in the blood?

lines.short: The good feelings fade within one dose and within three days; hunger stays gone.
lines.but: All of this used small oral doses in six to nine people in a laboratory.
how: Within one dose, the effects peak in about a quarter of an hour, then fade.
Over three days of twice-daily doses, the good feelings were gone by day three.
Eating stayed down over the three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew.
The body did not clear the drug faster; that was measured and had not changed.

cards.statement: When meth's good feelings fade over days of use, the bad effects fade too.

questions: Does MDMA stop working as well with regular use?

lines.short: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
lines.but: This comes from questionnaires, retold in one review; no laboratory study has tested it.
how: In surveys, most people say the first time was the strongest.
People who have used more say they take more tablets in a night.
Nobody checked what the tablets held, and different people were compared, not followed over time.
In one study, longer use did not go with more tablets.

cards.statement: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.

questions: Taken nightly, do benzodiazepine sleeping pills still impair driving the next morning?

lines.short: For most pills the morning effect seemed smaller after several nights than after the first, but for some it lasted or grew over a week.
lines.but: The studies were small and short, and none followed people for more than about two weeks.
how: Volunteers took a pill or a dummy pill every night for a few nights.
With flurazepam, driving got slightly worse over the week, not better.
Other pills behaved differently, so there is no single answer.

cards.statement: With one benzodiazepine sleeping pill, flurazepam, next-day driving got slightly worse over a week of nightly use, not better.

questions: Does believing you've had alcohol change how you act?

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

cards.statement: Thinking you've drunk alcohol, when you haven't, is enough to change your mood and memory.
In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.

questions: Does caffeine make you sharper, or just undo withdrawal?

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

cards.statement: In a lab study, caffeine made people who have it often more alert than people who rarely have it.
In one study, caffeine made people who often have it more alert than people who rarely do.
Caffeine makes people who rarely have it more alert.

questions: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely?

lines.short: Maybe. In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place. In people, nobody has tested it well. One study asked 10 overdose survivors what was different.
lines.but: That's 10 people's memories, about 5 years later, with nobody to compare them with. Only 3 of them recalled a new place or crowd.
how: The idea: the place, the people and the ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance, so it may be weaker somewhere new.
In rat studies from the same researcher, tolerance was weaker in a new place, and a large dose of heroin was more often deadly there. Rats aren't people.
Of 10 overdose survivors, 7 recalled something unusual that day: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. The other 3 recalled nothing unusual.
Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new without an overdose. A later review by the same researcher suggests a treatment based on the idea, but cites no test of it.

cards.statement: In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place than in the usual one.
It's been shown in people that using in a new place makes an overdose more likely.

questions: In MDMA deaths, which medicines were found too?

lines.short: Among 19 Australian deaths with MDMA and a risky mix, antidepressants, opioids and benzos were common.
lines.but: The 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the counts do not show how common any mix is.
how: In 14,682 coroners' cases (2002 to 2008), 106 had MDMA in the blood. Six in 10 of them died of injuries such as hanging or a crash, so MDMA in the blood does not show that it caused the death.
The authors rated 19 of the 106 as having a risky drug combination. Of those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine (benzo).
Four of them had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type. Three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died.

A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.

cards.statement: When MDMA is found in the blood of someone who died, it usually caused the death.

questions: What about MAOI antidepressants, like moclobemide?
MDMA with MAOI antidepressants such as moclobemide?

lines.short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.
lines.but: Four deaths cannot give a rate, and all four also had other drugs in their blood or urine.
how: None of the four had been prescribed moclobemide. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs.
The authors thought it was serotonin syndrome, but its defining signs were not recorded. MDMA levels were about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes.
Reviews rank MDMA with this kind of antidepressant as the highest-risk mix they list. Nobody has counted people who took both and had no such outcome.
Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more. No study measured what happens then with this antidepressant.

cards.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with moclobemide or similar antidepressants as the riskiest mix they list.

questions: What about other drugs that raise serotonin?
Which drugs add to MDMA's serotonin risk?

lines.short: One 2007 review ranked drugs by serotonin risk with ecstasy: MAOIs highest, SSRIs lower.
lines.but: This is the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work, not from counts of people.
how: Lower risk, the review says: SSRI-type antidepressants and a few painkillers and cough medicines, which it says weaken ecstasy's effects.
Middle: stimulants such as amphetamine and cocaine, and supplements such as tryptophan. Highest: MAOI antidepressants.
Deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are rare, the review says, but harm is more likely with other drugs that act on serotonin.
No study counted how often each mix causes harm. Some people feel little from an amount of ecstasy and take more; no study measured what that does to the risk.

cards.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.

questions: What happens with SSRI antidepressants?

lines.short: An SSRI muted MDMA's effects in lab tests; with paroxetine, MDMA blood levels rose.
lines.but: Only 28 healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most, and no one was given more MDMA.
how: 16 volunteers rated MDMA's effects about 60 percent lower after citalopram; their blood levels were not measured.
In 12 men, paroxetine lessened the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size. Yet the MDMA peak in the blood was about 1 in 6 higher.
Feeling little can have many reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here.
No one was given more MDMA once its effects were muted, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk.

cards.statement: An SSRI antidepressant that dulls MDMA's effects also lowers MDMA levels in your blood.

questions: What about other antidepressants?

lines.short: Other antidepressants did not act alike: some muted MDMA's effects, and bupropion did not.
lines.but: These numbers are second-hand, from a 2022 review of single trials with 16 healthy people each.
how: Duloxetine and reboxetine lowered MDMA's rated effects. The MDMA peak in the blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher.
Bupropion did not lower the ratings. The MDMA level was higher too (about 14 percent at the peak, 33 percent over the day), while heart rate rose less.

Some people feel little from an amount and take more. A slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ or a muting medicine can each be the reason. No trial tested what happened then.
The review's authors guess, without data, that bupropion with MDMA might raise the chance of seizures.

cards.statement: If an antidepressant mutes MDMA's effects, that means less MDMA is in your blood.

questions: What do case reports say about mixing with medicines?

lines.short: In safety reports, ecstasy cases that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often.
lines.but: Voluntary reports cannot show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.
how: In 946 US reports about ecstasy, those that also named an antidepressant had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome.
Reports naming other kinds of medicine had higher odds still: about 8 times for muscle relaxants and about 7 times for anesthetics.
In a survey of 216 adults, 76 in 100 who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria. They also reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness.
The review's authors suggest, without data, that people whose effects were muted may have taken more.

cards.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, cases that also named an antidepressant more often ended in death.

questions: What about other psychiatric medicines?

lines.short: Few other psychiatric medicines were tested with MDMA, and the results differ by medicine.
lines.but: Each was tested once in 14 to 16 healthy people, and the results come second-hand from a 2022 review.
how: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, did not change heart rate or blood pressure. It lowered well-being by about 31 percent and raised anxiety by about 47 percent.
Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rise in heart rate by about 79 percent.
The review found no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA.
A slow start, as with methylphenidate, can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. No trial tested what happens then.

cards.statement: Only a few psychiatric medicines have been tested together with MDMA in studies.

questions: Why do some bodies, or some medicines, make MDMA stronger?

lines.short: MDMA seems to switch off the enzyme that clears it, so body differences matter less.
lines.but: Only 7 people had no working enzyme, and no study gave a second dose of MDMA.
how: Among 139 volunteers in eight lab studies, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 had a peak MDMA level about 15 percent higher, in the first 3 hours only.
In 15 men, tests after one MDMA dose looked like those of people with no working enzyme in 10 of them. The enzyme had not fully recovered after 10 days.
Medicines that block the enzyme raised the MDMA peak by about 15 to 20 percent. Paroxetine raised it by 16 percent in 12 men.
Bodies that differ are one reason a person can feel little from an amount and take more. None of these studies gave a second dose, so what happens then is not known.

cards.statement: People with no working version of the enzyme that clears MDMA get far higher levels of it.

questions: Does one dose of meth make thinking worse at the time?

lines.short: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.
lines.but: The studies were small, so small or moderate harm can't be ruled out. Binges were not tested.
how: Lab studies gave people mostly single doses.
Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse. On some tasks people did better.
The studies were small. The two main ones, and the review of the others, came from one research group.
Binges and long-term use were not tested.

cards.statement: In lab studies, meth made attention and memory clearly worse at the time.

questions: Do 'smart drugs' like Adderall make healthy people smarter?

lines.short: Barely. A single pill of Adderall (amphetamine) or methylphenidate gave healthy adults at most a small lift on some lab tests. In one trial, people felt helped; scores didn't rise.
lines.but: These studies tested a single pill in a lab, in healthy volunteers. Daily use, studying and exams were not tested.
how: In a US trial, 46 healthy young adults took Adderall or a dummy pill on different test days. None of 13 tests improved.
They still rated the Adderall pill as more helpful than the dummy pill, but feeling helped was not clearly linked to scoring better.
Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response.
A bigger boost to memory tested hours or days later came mostly from one lab's studies of men. Adjusted for missing studies, it nearly halved.

cards.statement: Pills like Adderall give healthy people a big boost on thinking tests.
In one trial, healthy adults' test scores rose after taking Adderall.

questions: Is nitrous oxide (laughing gas) linked to nerve damage?

lines.short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.
lines.but: No doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common lasting numbness is after nitrous oxide.
how: A review pooled doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas): 57 had used it for fun, 25 in surgery.
80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Of 75 who had a spine scan, 51 showed a change in the spinal cord.
58 of 82 tested had low vitamin B12. But the search only found reports mentioning B12, so this is partly built in.
In an online survey, 200 of 4,633 people who used nitrous oxide in the past year reported numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks.

cards.statement: In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used nitrous oxide (laughing gas) in the past year reported lasting numbness.
In doctors' reports of health problems after laughing gas, most people had numbness or tingling.

questions: Is withdrawal from fentanyl worse than from heroin or other opioids?

lines.short: In one study, people coming off fentanyl had worse withdrawal than people coming off other opioids, such as heroin.
lines.but: The two groups were studied ten years apart, so something other than fentanyl may explain it.
how: 30 people who had used fentanyl were compared with 103 people who had used heroin or similar drugs ten years earlier.
Both groups got the same medicine on the same research ward, but only the fentanyl group could also get extra medicines for symptoms.
The fentanyl group's withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, while the other group's eased from the start.
A fast heartbeat happened to 43 in 100 in the fentanyl group, against 19 in 100 in the other group.

cards.statement: In one study, fentanyl withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, unlike heroin-type withdrawal.

questions: Do fentanyl test strips show fentanyl when it is there?

lines.short: Almost always, in lab tests: 98 in 100 seized drug samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip.
lines.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.

cards.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.

questions: Do nitazene test strips work?

lines.short: Mostly, in the lab. They picked up 24 of 33 kinds of nitazene but missed most desnitazenes, so a negative doesn't rule nitazenes out.
lines.but: Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested, not mixed street drugs.
how: One lab tried 33 kinds of nitazene. The strips picked up 24. They missed 6 of the 7 desnitazenes, even at high strength.
Six nearly pure powders from the drug market all showed up.
A second lab found the strips did not react to 76 other drugs and cutting agents.
No study we read tested street drugs where a nitazene is a small part of a mix. So how often strips get it wrong on real samples is unknown.

cards.statement: Nitazene test strips pick up every kind of nitazene.

questions: Do xylazine test strips work?

lines.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
lines.but: It's one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment, not powders or pills.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.

cards.statement: Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, can also make xylazine test strips read positive.
A negative xylazine test strip means there's no xylazine.

questions: Do take-home fentanyl strips match what trained staff find?

lines.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
lines.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In British Columbia in 2019, people took strips from ten harm-reduction sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 on site; cocaine, 17 against 1. The authors think most extra positives were false, but didn't test it.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.

cards.statement: With opioids, take-home fentanyl strips showed fentanyl about as often as staff tests on site.

questions: Are heroin overdose deaths always caused by heroin alone?

lines.short: Not necessarily. Older studies often found other drugs too: alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100 of these deaths. But finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.
lines.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours, and other people were often there: more than half the time, in four studies. These come second-hand, from a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classed 23 in 100 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners as something other than a direct overdose, like an infection, an injury, or drug effects plus an illness.
Heroin use can also be missed, because its marker can fall after death. Levels also depend on where and when samples are taken.

cards.statement: Heroin overdose deaths are almost always instant.

questions: How many people who use stimulants like meth get hooked?

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

cards.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
A US survey found tobacco hooked a bigger share of people who'd used it than cocaine or meth-like stimulants.

questions: Can people become dependent on ecstasy?

lines.short: Yes, some do. How many depends on who's asked: about 4 in 100 people who'd used it recently in US surveys, but up to 73 in 100 in small groups.
lines.but: Every checklist was made for other drugs, and most studies used volunteers, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy.
how: In two US surveys of the general public, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. Among clubgoers, young people in detention and volunteers, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

The symptoms reported most included carrying on despite problems, lots of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.

cards.statement: In the one study that followed people dependent on ecstasy, 93 in 100 were no longer dependent about three years later.

questions: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?

lines.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated. In a US survey, 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent about 3 years later.
lines.but: How many depends on who is counted, and in the studies we read, recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers back from Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics there, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some may still have had one or two, and treatment in between wasn't reported.

Across 21 studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, depending on how deaths and dropouts are counted. For many, the authors say, the problem is long-lasting.

For alcohol, figures for recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because studies count different groups. Many who recovered were never treated. Far fewer of everyone with a problem recover untreated in a year.

cards.statement: In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent three years later.
Most US soldiers who were hooked on narcotics in Vietnam stayed hooked after coming home.

questions: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?

lines.short: Possibly, though it's the same drug. People new to crack reported each sign of dependence more often: about 18 to 32 in 100, against 5 to 12 for powder.
lines.but: Each person was asked once, so the surveys cannot show that crack itself is the reason.
how: Powder can't be smoked; crack is. A 1996 review links most differences to how each is taken, how fast and how much cocaine that delivers, and how much people use, not the form itself.
In US surveys from 1995 to 1998, about 18 to 32 in 100 people who had just started crack reported each sign of dependence. For people who had just started powder, it was 5 to 12 in 100.
After allowing for how many days people had used, and for age, drinking, smoking and injecting, the gap was smaller but did not go away.
A review of 302 studies found comparisons of crack with other cocaine mixed. Its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it.

cards.statement: Crack and powder cocaine are two different drugs.
Research shows crack cocaine itself directly causes the infections and violence linked to it.

questions: How fast can you get hooked on cocaine?

lines.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
lines.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence. So did about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.

cards.statement: Most people who start using cocaine are hooked within a year.

questions: Do people who use ecstasy score lower on memory tests?

lines.short: On average, people who use ecstasy score lower on some memory and thinking tests.
lines.but: The studies disagree a lot, and none can show that ecstasy caused it.
how: Two reviews looked at small studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who do not.
Scores were lower on average, but results differed so much between studies that the size is uncertain.
Almost everyone in these studies also used other drugs, most often cannabis.
Everyone was tested after they had started, so the difference may have been there first.

cards.statement: In studies linking ecstasy to lower memory scores, almost everyone also used other drugs, most often cannabis.

questions: Does memory recover after people stop using ecstasy?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether scores recover after people stop using ecstasy.
lines.but: The studies compared different people, not the same people over time.
how: A review pooled a few small studies of people who had stopped for at least 6 months.
They scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used.
Breaks longer than 6 months were not tested, although the review's summary says otherwise.
Most of the studies were rated poor quality.

cards.statement: Once people stop using ecstasy, their test scores bounce back, research shows.

questions: Do brain scans show serotonin changes in people who use ecstasy?

lines.short: Scans show less of a serotonin marker in people who use ecstasy.
lines.but: Nobody in these studies was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.
how: The marker sits on the endings of serotonin nerve cells in the brain.
Four teams used the same scan and all found less of it in the outer brain.
Deeper parts of the brain mostly looked the same as in other people.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.

cards.statement: Brain scans prove that ecstasy destroys serotonin nerve cells.

questions: What happened to the famous 2002 study claiming ecstasy damaged monkeys' brains?

lines.short: A 2002 study said ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains. It was withdrawn a year later.
lines.but: Fewer newspapers told readers about the mistake than told the first story.
how: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle.
Two of the ten animals given the drug died during the study.
Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.
The notice does not say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

cards.statement: When a 2002 study on ecstasy and monkeys' brains was withdrawn, more big US newspapers reported the withdrawal than the study.
The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.

questions: Does ecstasy damage dopamine nerve cells?

lines.short: It has not been shown that ecstasy harms dopamine nerve cells in people.
lines.but: Very little has been measured in people, so this does not show it is safe.
how: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn: the animals got a different drug.
A review found five human scan studies, and none showed a clear dopamine change.
In one, the dopamine marker was lower only in people who had also used amphetamine recently.
A by-product in spinal fluid cannot show whether nerve cells were harmed.

cards.statement: Ecstasy has been shown to damage dopamine nerve cells in people.

questions: Does ecstasy harm the brain for good?

lines.short: Experts disagree about whether ecstasy leaves lasting harm to the serotonin system.
lines.but: Almost nobody was scanned before they started, so a difference may have come first.
how: Four teams scanned people who use ecstasy and found less of a serotonin marker.
The one study that scanned people before their first use found no change.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.
Nobody has been scanned while using and again years after stopping.

cards.statement: Ecstasy has been proven to cause lasting brain damage in people.

questions: After stopping ecstasy, do serotonin changes on scans return to normal?

lines.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
lines.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.

cards.statement: The serotonin changes seen on scans of people who used ecstasy are known to be permanent.

questions: What does MDMA do to body temperature, heart and blood pressure?

lines.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: 136 healthy adults got one lab dose. The top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.

cards.statement: MDMA only raises body temperature when people dance in hot, crowded places.

questions: Is low blood salt after MDMA more common in women?

lines.short: Yes, among people who got ill: 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men, in one poison-centre study.
lines.but: It counts only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Only 188 of 545 people in California poison-centre records had a blood salt test. Of 105 women tested, 55 had a low level; of 83 men, 18 did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.
A review describes 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount: a marker of a water-holding hormone rose only in women, with no clear difference reported in the hormone or blood salt.

cards.statement: Among people who got ill after MDMA, low blood salt was more common in women than men.

questions: Does taking more MDMA raise blood levels more than you'd expect?

lines.short: Yes, it seems so: a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher, and about twice the total over the day.
lines.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
The kidneys cleared MDMA at the same pace at both doses; the rest of the body cleared it about half as fast at the larger one.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

People can feel little from an amount for several reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ. Some take more. These studies didn't test that.

questions: What does smoking cannabis do to the lungs?

lines.short: Smoking cannabis is linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze; light smoking didn't lower lung function.
lines.but: Many people also smoked tobacco, so the studies can't say how much comes from cannabis.
how: In two long-running studies, breathing symptoms eased in people who stopped.
In a 20-year study of about 5,000 adults, light cannabis smoking did not lower lung function; tobacco did.
Too few people smoked cannabis heavily for years to know what that does.
In one study, symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, but it had no comparison group.

questions: Are edibles a danger to young children?

lines.short: Calls to US poison centres about young children eating edibles rose about 15 times over, 2017 to 2021.
lines.but: These are only the calls that were made, and the study can't say why the number rose.
how: Most of the children were 1 to 4 years old and ate the edible at home.
More than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital, and 35 needed a breathing tube. No deaths were reported.
The authors suggest changes in the law, the pandemic or more calling, but the data can't separate these.

questions: Do cannabis or CBD products taken by mouth help people sleep?

lines.short: In sleep labs, cannabis taken by mouth did not reliably change sleep, compared with a dummy pill or with sleep before treatment.
lines.but: Most were CBD or mild THC medicines for people with sleep problems; smoking was not tested.
how: Six studies compared cannabis medicines swallowed by mouth with a dummy pill (placebo) or with sleep before treatment.
Sleep length, time to fall asleep, waking in the night and deep sleep did not change.
Results for dream (REM) sleep did not agree with each other.
Small early studies (1972 to 1982), mostly with high doses of THC, often found less dream sleep.

cards.statement: Sleep-lab studies found cannabis taken by mouth helps people fall asleep faster.

questions: Is the day after worse with synthetic cannabis than with ordinary cannabis?

lines.short: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover.
lines.but: These are memories from a 2011 online survey; nobody tested the products.
how: About a thousand people who had used both compared them in an online survey.
They said synthetic cannabis made it harder to get on with things afterwards.
They said it gave more bad feelings and fear of others while high, and much less enjoyment.
Most preferred ordinary cannabis, and said synthetic cannabis wore off sooner.

cards.statement: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover than ordinary cannabis.
People who've used both say synthetic cannabis is as enjoyable as ordinary cannabis.

questions: Do cannabis medicines help sleep, anxiety, appetite or other conditions?

lines.short: Too few small trials to tell; sleep scores were slightly better than with a dummy.
lines.but: Each condition had only a few small trials. Many had serious weaknesses.
how: In trials for pain or MS, sleep scores were a little better with the medicine than with a dummy (placebo). This evidence is very weak.
Anxiety, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome had only one or two small trials each. Appetite in HIV had four.
No trial treated depression. In trials for other illnesses, depression scores mostly did not differ.
Epilepsy was not part of this review. Trials of a CBD medicine for epilepsy were not read for this answer.

cards.statement: Trials show cannabis medicines help with anxiety and depression.

questions: Does CBD taken with THC change THC's effects?

lines.short: Studies disagree on CBD and THC; no reliable pattern has been shown across different conditions.
lines.but: The studies used different amounts and timings. Most were small, and earlier trials were read through a review.
how: A review gathered 16 lab studies of healthy volunteers, from 1974 to 2019. In most, adding CBD made no clear difference to feeling high, heart rate or THC in the blood.
A few small studies, where THC was swallowed or injected, found less anxiety or fewer paranoid feelings with CBD. The review found no pattern by amount or way of taking it.
In a later trial, 18 adults ate brownies with THC alone or the same THC plus a large amount of CBD. With CBD, blood THC was higher and they felt sicker and more impaired.
Other test medicines, including a sedative, were given in that trial. They may have added to the effects.

cards.statement: CBD reliably weakens the high from THC, the main active part of cannabis.

questions: Can I get flashbacks after LSD or psilocybin?

lines.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
lines.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.

cards.statement: In lab studies, about 1 in 11 volunteers reported a short flashback after LSD or psilocybin.
A psychedelic flashback means reliving the whole trip for hours.

questions: Do people feel low a few days after taking ecstasy?

lines.short: Two small studies disagree, so they cannot say how often a mid-week low happens.
lines.but: Both studies were small, and only one measured people before they took ecstasy.
how: A London study found people who took ecstasy felt sadder mid-week than people who only drank alcohol.
That study did not measure anyone before the night out, and did not count how many felt low.
A Melbourne study measured people a week before and found no difference from people who use ecstasy but skipped it.
In that study, people who slept badly felt worse, looking at both groups together.

cards.statement: Research shows most people feel a mid-week low a few days after taking ecstasy.

questions: Is using LSD, mushrooms or mescaline linked to mental health problems?

lines.short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.
lines.but: People were asked once, so the survey can't show whether LSD, mushrooms or mescaline cause or prevent problems.
how: 130,152 US adults answered private computer questions at home in 2001 to 2004; 21,967 had ever used LSD, mushrooms, mescaline or peyote.
At first glance, all 20 mental health measures were 2 to 3 times as common in people who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline.
Those who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline used far more other drugs: 98 in 100 had used cannabis, against 33 in 100 of others.
Once that, risk-taking, stressful events and background were counted, no measure was higher for LSD, mushrooms or mescaline. A few were lower, maybe by chance.

cards.statement: In a US survey, people who used LSD or mushrooms still had more mental health problems once other differences were counted.

questions: Do clonidine or lofexidine help with opioid withdrawal?

lines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, fewer people had bad withdrawal and more finished treatment.
lines.but: Only three small, old trials, mostly in hospital, and none with people coming off fentanyl.
how: Three trials gave people coming off heroin either the medicine or a dummy pill, picked by chance.
Bad withdrawal happened to about 19 in 100 on the medicine and about 59 in 100 on the dummy pill.
About 56 in 100 finished treatment on the medicine, against 29 in 100 on the dummy pill.
The medicine made some people sleepy or dizzy and lowered their blood pressure.

cards.statement: Clonidine and lofexidine barely help with heroin withdrawal.

questions: Does buprenorphine help people get through opioid withdrawal better than clonidine?

lines.short: Yes: more people finished withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine.
lines.but: No trial reported people coming off fentanyl, and two stopped early, which may have skewed the results.
how: Fourteen trials put people coming off opioids, mostly heroin, on buprenorphine or on clonidine or lofexidine, by chance.
About 72 in 100 finished treatment on buprenorphine, against about 45 in 100 on the other medicines.
On buprenorphine, withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed in treatment longer than on the other medicines.
There was no clear difference in how many had side effects, but they differed: headache with buprenorphine, dizziness and dry mouth with clonidine.

cards.statement: More people finish opioid withdrawal treatment on buprenorphine than on clonidine or lofexidine.

questions: Will I sleep badly when I stop cannabis?

lines.short: Studies in one review found that many people who used cannabis regularly sleep badly after stopping, often with strange dreams.
lines.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Studies asked people how they slept after stopping regular cannabis, and some recorded their sleep in a lab.
Between about a third and three quarters of those with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks.
In the lab they took longer to fall asleep and woke up more than before they stopped.
Poor sleep was linked with going back to cannabis.

cards.statement: Stopping regular cannabis use can mess with your sleep and bring strange dreams.

questions: How common is withdrawal when people who use cannabis regularly stop, and what is it like?
How common is cannabis withdrawal, and what is it like?

lines.short: About 17 in 100 in general surveys; more than half in clinic and hospital groups.
lines.but: Studies counted it in different ways, and none checked how often people get these feelings anyway.
how: A 2020 review pooled 50 groups of people who used cannabis regularly or had a use disorder.
Withdrawal means at least 3 of 7 problems within about a week of stopping heavy use: irritability, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood or body symptoms such as headache.
Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks; one statement says it can last about a month.
Counted person by person, about 28 in 100 in the review had withdrawal; its headline of 47 in 100 mostly reflects small clinic groups.

cards.statement: There is no such thing as cannabis withdrawal.

questions: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?

lines.short: Yes, some do. People judged a person more harshly when their troubles were said to come from drug use, not a health concern.
lines.but: These are views given after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, couldn't take part.
When Alex's trouble was put down to drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted much more distance and saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money game, they took slightly more from Alex.
Calling it a brain disease instead of a problem made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested labels on about 500 people at mental health conferences. Those whose story called a man a substance abuser, not someone with a substance use disorder, agreed slightly more with blaming and punishing him. It's a shaky result.

cards.statement: In one experiment, describing a person's trouble as 'drug use', not a 'health concern', made readers see them as more dangerous.

questions: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?

lines.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
lines.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.

cards.statement: In a UK study, readers judged a man who died from drugs more harshly than a woman.

questions: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently?

lines.short: Many health workers said they felt negative. Whether care was worse is not clear.
lines.but: Mostly surveys of what workers said, from 2000 to 2011, in a few countries.
how: A review gathered 28 studies, mostly from Australia, the UK and the US. In them, health workers described their views of patients with drug or alcohol problems.

Many workers felt negative about these patients, or less positive than about people with other illnesses. This was more common outside drug and alcohol services. Some studies found neutral or positive views.
Only a few studies asked whether this changes care, and they disagreed. In one, people who felt staff treated them unfairly were less likely to finish treatment.
In another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care. The one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.

cards.statement: The one study that watched real health care visits found worse care for patients with drug or alcohol problems.

questions: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?

lines.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
lines.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published 1991 to 2002, of 11,505 students in grades 5 to 12, comparing those who had DARE with those who didn't.
Students who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as others. The studies checked from right after the classes to 10 years later.
In 8 of the 11 studies, the result couldn't be told apart from no difference. Two small ones found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more.
Four results, including the only 10-year one, weren't worked out but filled in as zero.

cards.statement: Kids who had the original DARE classes went on to use less alcohol, tobacco and drugs than other kids.

questions: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?

lines.short: No sign they did. Despite nearly $1 billion from Congress, teens' reported cannabis use stayed flat in a national survey, and those who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
lines.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens said they'd ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.

cards.statement: The US government's anti-drug ads of 1999 to 2004 cut cannabis use among teens.
Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.

questions: Is strong cannabis more closely linked to psychosis than weaker cannabis?

lines.short: Daily use of strong types had the strongest link with psychosis, but the gap from weaker types could be chance.
lines.but: Strength was guessed from the type people named, and both studies come from one team.
how: Two studies by one team, one in south London and one in 11 places in Europe and Brazil, compared people who had a first psychosis with people from the same areas who had not.

In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong types (10% THC or more on average) went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis, compared with never using. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times; the gap between the two could be chance.

In the 11 places, using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis. In London, using strong types less than once a week went with nearly 2 times the odds, but some numbers in that study do not add up. In both studies, weaker types were not linked once all patterns of use were counted together.
Nobody tested the cannabis: people named the type they had used after they became ill, and its strength was taken from police, European and national figures.

cards.statement: In two studies linking strong cannabis to psychosis, researchers tested the cannabis people had used.
In one study, daily use of strong cannabis went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis.

questions: Is cannabis stronger than it used to be?

lines.short: Yes, on average. In cannabis from 7 countries, 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash.
lines.but: Most samples were cannabis seized by police, not picked at random, so they may not match what people buy.
how: Researchers combined 12 studies from 7 countries that measured THC in cannabis. Most tested police seizures; two Dutch studies bought samples at random in shops.
A point is a share of the weight: 5% to 6% THC is one point. These numbers describe the cannabis, not what people took in.
Not everywhere: US weed rose in every period studied, but weed in the UK (1975–1989) and New Zealand (1979–1996) showed no clear rise.
CBD, another substance in cannabis, did not change. The authors put the weed rise down to stronger kinds selling more, but sales were not measured.

cards.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.

questions: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed?

lines.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
lines.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed made people feel.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples from licensed growers in six US states, 2013 to 2021. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name. They didn't check whether the labels differed in THC or CBD.

In 41,201 samples where THC outweighed CBD, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.

cards.statement: Indica and sativa labels tell you which smell compounds your weed has.

questions: Why do psychedelic visuals look like tunnels, spirals and honeycombs?

lines.short: Maybe the visual brain's own wiring. A maths model shows how tunnels, spirals, cobwebs and honeycombs could arise there. It wasn't tested in people on a drug.
lines.but: It's only maths: the drug is just a setting for how excitable the brain is. The match was judged by eye against a few drawings.
how: People see simple shapes after LSD or cannabis. They also come with flickering light or when falling asleep. An earlier researcher sorted these into four types: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals.
The wiring from eye to brain turns a tunnel or a spiral into plain stripes. These run across the brain's first area for sight.
In the model, when that area gets too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form by themselves, shaped by how its cells connect. Mapped back to what you'd see, they look like all four types.
The wiring data came mostly from cats and monkeys. The best matches needed wider connections than that anatomy shows, and some complex visions don't fit the model.

cards.statement: The simple shapes people see on LSD have been sorted into just four types.
It's proven that trip tunnels and spirals come from the brain's wiring.

questions: Does hot-pepper (capsaicin) cream ease cannabis-linked vomiting in hospital?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet: in small studies it sometimes helped and sometimes did not.
lines.but: One small fair test and four weaker studies, mostly at moderate to high risk of bias.
how: Cannabis hyperemesis means being sick again and again in some people who use a lot of cannabis.
In one small fair test, the cream did not ease sickness more than a dummy cream at the first check.
A few more people felt fully better with the cream, and sickness was lower at a later check.
Other studies disagreed; in one, more people given the cream than not given it were admitted to hospital, a difference that could be chance.

questions: Do medicines that block dopamine ease cannabis-linked vomiting in hospital?

lines.short: In two small studies, haloperidol eased sickness more than a usual anti-sickness medicine, and people given haloperidol or droperidol went home sooner than people given other care.
lines.but: Only two small studies, and both medicines can cause sudden muscle spasms.
how: In a small fair test, haloperidol was compared with a usual anti-sickness medicine (ondansetron).
With haloperidol, pain and sickness eased more and people left hospital sooner.
In hospital records, people given droperidol left sooner than people not given it.
A few people had sudden muscle spasms (dystonia) after these medicines.

questions: Do people who use cannabis often do worse on memory and thinking tests?

lines.short: On average they score a little lower than people who use little or none.
lines.but: People were tested only after they had started, so the studies can't show that cannabis caused it.
how: A review pooled 69 studies of young people, about 21 years old on average, who used cannabis often.
They scored a little lower on learning, memory, attention and planning tests. Language, shape and movement tests showed no clear gap.
The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days before the test, and bigger in people getting help for their cannabis use. Small studies found bigger gaps.
In a British twin study, the gap at age 18 was no longer clear when each twin was compared with their own twin.

cards.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.

questions: What side effects do cannabis medicines cause?

lines.short: More side effects than with a dummy, such as dizziness, feeling high, confusion and dry mouth.
lines.but: Short trials at the highest dose tested; long-term harms were not studied.
how: Researchers put together trials of cannabis medicines. They were compared with a dummy (placebo) or another medicine, at the highest dose each trial gave.
About 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one side effect. So did 62 in 100 on the comparison.
The odds of quitting a trial because of side effects were about three times higher, and of a serious side effect 1.4 times. Deaths did not differ.
The review gave counts out of 100 only for having any side effect, not for each one.

cards.statement: Cannabis medicines have hardly any side effects.

questions: Are frequent use and starting young linked to cannabis dependence?

lines.short: People who use more often are more often dependent; for starting young, studies disagree.
lines.but: Most numbers come second-hand from reviews, and none can show what causes what.
how: Reviews give figures from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2 for people who use daily; one often-quoted figure (25 to 50 in 100) cannot be traced to any study.
Reviews say about 1 in 6 people who start as teenagers become dependent, against about 1 in 10 of everyone who has used.
In a large US survey, starting before 14 went with more dependence until other mental health and drug problems were counted, then with less; that does not mean starting early protects.
Dependence partly means using more than you meant to, so using often and being dependent are hard to pull apart.

cards.statement: You can't become dependent on cannabis, even if you use it every day.

questions: What is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (repeated severe vomiting), and does stopping end it?

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

cards.statement: Regular cannabis use can come with bouts of severe vomiting that ended when people stopped, in most reported cases.
In published cases of repeated vomiting with regular cannabis use, most people found hot baths or showers eased it for a while.

questions: Can cannabis cause psychosis, and does using it daily matter?

lines.short: People who use cannabis, most of all daily, get psychosis more often than people who don't.
lines.but: This is a link: these studies cannot show that cannabis was the cause.
how: Seven big studies followed young people for years. Those who had ever used cannabis had about 1.4 times the odds of psychosis later, mostly symptoms rather than a diagnosed illness, compared with people who never had.

For each study's heaviest-use group (from more than 50 times to daily use or dependence), the odds were about twice as high. In two studies of people with a first psychosis, daily use went with about 3 times the odds, and using now and then was not linked.

In a big Swedish study of men, about 6 in 1,000 who had never used cannabis, and about 38 in 1,000 who had used it more than 50 times, later went to hospital with schizophrenia. These counts do not allow for other differences between the men.
Taking other differences between people into account, such as other drug use and other mental health problems, shrank the link by about half.

cards.statement: Most men who used cannabis heavily never went to hospital with schizophrenia, in a big Swedish study.

questions: Is teenage cannabis use linked to depression or anxiety later?

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most were a bit more often depressed later than teens who didn't.
lines.but: These studies can't show that cannabis caused it; other differences between the teens may explain it.
how: Seven long-term studies followed teens who did and did not use cannabis until they were young adults.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. The studies did not say how many in 100 became depressed.
The studies took into account how depressed or anxious the teens were at the start, but not always tobacco or other drugs.
Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only three studies measured it.

cards.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis are a bit more likely to be depressed as young adults.

questions: Do cannabis medicines help long-lasting pain?

lines.short: Slightly: about half a point less pain out of 10 than with a dummy medicine.
lines.but: The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with long-lasting pain got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
Pain scores were about half a point lower out of 10 with the medicine.
37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%; this difference may be due to chance.
Most of the combined trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, and none lasted more than 15 weeks.

cards.statement: Cannabis medicines work much better than a dummy medicine for long-lasting pain.

questions: Do medicines for constipation caused by opioids work?

lines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, more people's constipation got better.
lines.but: Nearly all the trials were in people taking opioids for pain; only one also included people dependent on opioids, so they say little about people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment.
how: 27 trials gave people either a medicine or a dummy pill, chosen by chance.
About 52 in 100 got better on a medicine, against 33 in 100 on the dummy pill.
In separate trials against a dummy pill, medicines that block opioids in the gut did better than the prescription laxative lubiprostone; no trial compared them directly.
Diarrhoea and tummy pain were more common on the medicines than on the dummy pill, and slightly more people stopped them because of side effects (about 7 in 100 against 5 in 100).

questions: Does using cannabis as a teenager lower IQ later in life?

lines.short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.
lines.but: Other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of lighter use found no clear extra loss.
how: In New Zealand, 874 people took IQ tests as children and again at 38.
The 38 people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. People who never used gained a little.
Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern. The first team found that family background did not change their result.
In US and British twin studies, mostly of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more than the twin who did not. These studies could miss a small loss.

cards.statement: In twin studies of mostly light teen use, the twin who used cannabis lost clearly more IQ than the other.
Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.

questions: Is teenage cannabis use linked to suicidal thoughts or attempts?

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.
lines.but: Only three studies each, mostly measured in the teen years; they cannot show cause.
how: A review combined three long-term studies on suicidal thoughts and three on suicide attempts.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and about 3.5 times the odds of attempts, compared with teens who did not use cannabis.
In two of the three studies for each, this was measured while the young people were still teenagers.
In other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were taken into account.

cards.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.

questions: Does drinking at a young age lead to alcohol problems later on?

lines.short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.
lines.but: Only a few small studies followed young people over time; the big survey relied on memory.
how: In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who started drinking at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. They had to remember their first drink.
A review found only four groups of young people whose first drink was recorded as teenagers and who were followed into adulthood.
Drinking early went with more drinking problems in some of them. In others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems, were taken into account.

In US twins, the twin who drank without permission by about 15 drank more as an adult than the other twin, even in identical twins. But in identical twins it was not clearly linked to signs of an alcohol disorder.

cards.statement: Starting to drink alcohol young has been shown to cause alcohol problems later in life.
People who had their first drink at 14 or younger more often had alcohol dependence than late starters.

questions: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later?

lines.short: People who started young more often had drug or drinking problems later on.
lines.but: Studies can't show that starting young is the cause. Much of the link runs in families.
