lines.but: Three cases, with no comparison between treatments or with no treatment.
how: Two men were given medicines for psychosis, which did not visibly help.
The third man's medicine was stopped after he had fits.
One man calmed down when he was put in a dim, quiet room.
All three got better within a few weeks, one after he left hospital.

cards.statement: In one reported case, a man in a long breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP calmed in a dim, quiet room.

questions: What happens to your sleep when you stop using a lot of cannabis?

lines.short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.
lines.but: Three small studies, two of them from the 1970s with very strong lab doses.
how: Sleep was measured in a lab while people were still using cannabis and after they stopped.
After stopping, they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream (REM) sleep.
The pooled data came from the first week after stopping, so this review cannot say how long the changes last.

cards.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.

questions: If people are given test strips, do they use them?

lines.short: It varies a lot. In different places, from 1 in 100 to 77 in 100.
lines.but: This is what people said or what services wrote down. Nobody checked.
how: In a paid study in Rhode Island in 2017, 62 of the 81 young adults who came back and were counted said they used at least one of their ten strips.
At a supervised injection site in Vancouver, staff offered a check on every visit. About 1 visit in 100 included one.
A review gives figures of 1 to 80 in 100. But these mostly count people who had used strips before a study began, not people the study gave strips to.
One programme did not report how many kits it gave out, so how many were used is unknown.

cards.statement: At a Vancouver supervised injection site offering a fentanyl check every visit, about 1 visit in 100 included one.

questions: What do people do when a strip shows fentanyl?

lines.short: Some say they use less or go slower; many keep the same amount.
lines.but: This is what people said or planned. Nobody watched what they actually did.
how: In a 2023 US study of 541 people, most strip results were followed by using the same amount.
In that study, 23 in 100 results with no fentanyl were followed by using more. For results with fentanyl, it was 6 in 100.
In Rhode Island and Baltimore, 45 in 100 and 31 in 100 of people whose strip showed fentanyl said they used a smaller amount.
No study compared people given strips with people who were not given them.

cards.statement: Studies have compared people given fentanyl test strips with people not given them, to see what strips change.

questions: Do people who use test strips have fewer overdoses?

lines.short: No one knows yet. One study found no clear difference over four weeks.
lines.but: The result was too uncertain to rule out fewer or more overdoses.
how: One US study followed 732 people at harm-reduction sites for four weeks in 2023. Once other differences were allowed for, overdoses that people survived were about as common in people who used strips as in those who did not.
That comparison also allowed for safety steps people took during the study, which could hide a difference. Before anything was allowed for, overdoses looked twice as common in people who used strips.

In Baltimore, 103 women were given strips, and 68 were asked again about 8 weeks later. 6 said they had an overdose in the month before the start, and 1 in the month before the last visit. There was no comparison group, and women who used no strips also reported fewer.
A review of 91 research papers found only two that looked at overdoses, and neither compared people who tested with people who did not.

cards.statement: People who use fentanyl test strips have been shown to have fewer overdoses.

questions: Do people keep using test strips over time?

lines.short: In the one study that lasted a year, fewer people had used a strip in the past month by the end than at the start.
lines.but: Many people left the study, and it did not find out why use fell.
how: 541 people who inject drugs, met at two services that give out clean needles in rural North Carolina and West Virginia, answered surveys at the start, after 6 months and after 12 months.
After a year, people were less likely than at the first survey to have used a strip in the past month. At 6 months there was no clear change.
Even so, more people had tried strips at some point: 65 in 100 at the first survey and 80 in 100 a year later, among those who answered all three surveys.
In two shorter studies, about 95 in 100 said they would use strips again. That is a plan, not a measure of use.

cards.statement: In the one year-long study of fentanyl test strips, recent strip use rose between the start and the end.

questions: Are people who use test strips different from people who don't?

lines.short: Yes. In the largest US study, they more often injected and used fentanyl.
lines.but: This is what people said, and most were already using drug services.
how: At US sites that hand out strips, 75 in 100 people who had used strips had injected in the past month, against 57 in 100 who had not.

In the same study, people who used strips already said they did more to lower their risk before it began. For example, 64 in 100 said they always had naloxone nearby when they used drugs, against 39 in 100 people who did not use strips.
Their overdose rate looked twice as high before anything was allowed for, and not clearly different after.
In a rural US study, people who had seen an overdose were more likely to use strips. In a small study, the two groups differed little.

cards.statement: At first glance, people who used fentanyl test strips in the largest US study looked twice as likely to overdose.

questions: Did US states that legalised test strips see fewer drug deaths?

lines.short: After the law, drug deaths ran about 3 a year per 100,000 people below other states' trend.
lines.but: It looked at laws, not at people using strips. Other changes at the same time could explain it.
how: Researchers used death records from every US state from 2018 to 2022. They counted 15 states and Washington, DC as making the strips legal in that time.

After the law, there were about 3 fewer drug deaths a year for every 100,000 people, about 7 in 100 fewer than expected. Once age, rural living and income were allowed for, this was about the same for White and Black people, though less certain for Black people.
The study did not check whether more people got or used strips. It counted deaths from any drug, and the drop came in the very first month of each law.

The researchers chose the law dates themselves. They kept Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico among the states without a law, though laws started there in 2021 and 2022, and moved two other dates later. They showed no results with their source's dates.

cards.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.

questions: Do people who drink a little live longer than people who don't drink?

lines.short: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths. Compared with people who never drank, there was no clear difference.
lines.but: Few studies made that comparison. So a small gain or a small loss is still possible.
how: Researchers put together dozens of studies. These followed millions of people for years and counted who died.
In most studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill. People who had stopped died more often.
Six studies started with younger people and compared them with people who had never drunk. There, people who drank a little died about as often.
Allowing for how the studies differed also shrank the gap. Researchers still disagree, and studies like these cannot show whether alcohol itself helps or harms.

cards.statement: In many alcohol studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill.
Studies show people who drink a little live longer than people who never drank.

questions: Is there an amount of alcohol with no health risk?

lines.short: Under 40, overall risk was lowest with almost no alcohol. Over 40, one model said half to two thirds of a drink a day.
lines.but: These are averages for whole populations, not one person's risk, and the over-40 dip rests on heart findings that gene studies mostly did not find.
how: Researchers built world models that added up the risks of 22 or 23 diseases and injuries linked to alcohol. A drink here means 10 grams of alcohol.
For young people, much of this illness is injuries, and injury risk rose with any drinking. Older people have more heart disease, where some studies saw lower risk with small amounts.
The lowest point is where gains for some illnesses balance losses for others. In the older model, the risk of every cancer it looked at still rose with drinking.
The models describe whole populations, not one person. They left out drinking a lot on some days.

cards.statement: In one world model, the risk of every cancer it looked at rose with drinking.

questions: At what amount does drinking start to shorten life?

lines.short: Deaths rose above about 100 grams of alcohol a week. The comparison was with very light drinking.
lines.but: People who drank more also smoked more. The studies could only partly allow for that.
how: Researchers pooled 83 studies of about 600,000 people who drank and had no known heart disease. They followed them for about 7 years.
They compared people with those who drank least (up to 25 grams a week), not with people who did not drink. 100 grams a week is about 14 grams a day.
The researchers used a model for 40-year-olds. Those drinking more than 350 grams a week could expect 4 to 5 fewer years of life than those drinking up to 100 grams.
Other studies compared with people who did not drink. They found more deaths in their groups drinking 45 grams a day or more, but their groups were too broad to show where the rise begins.

questions: Do people who drink a little have less heart disease?

lines.short: In many studies, people who drank a little had less heart disease than people who didn't.
lines.but: The group who didn't drink included people who had stopped, perhaps because they were ill, so alcohol may not be the reason.
how: Researchers pooled dozens of long studies. They asked adults how much they drank, then counted heart disease over the years.
People who drank had about a quarter lower risk than people who didn't. No study said how many people out of 100 that is.
Compared with people who had never drunk, men's heart deaths at one or two drinks a day were not clearly lower.
In a large UK study, the gap at moderate drinking was no longer clear once smoking, weight, exercise, diet and health were counted. The gene studies we read did not find the gap.

cards.statement: Drinking a little alcohol has been shown to protect the heart.

questions: Do gene studies back the idea that alcohol protects the heart?

lines.short: The gene studies we read did not find that drinking a little protects the heart.
lines.but: Gene studies have possible biases of their own, and they cannot show what small amounts do.
how: Some people carry genes that make them drink a bit less, or more. Researchers compared heart disease between these groups.
In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking less went with slightly less heart disease, not more.
In a large study of Chinese men, genes for drinking more made no clear difference to heart attacks, though a small effect either way cannot be ruled out.

Three researchers argue that gene studies can be misled, for example by family background or by heavy drinking days. They did not measure how much, and they note some Asian gene studies pointing the other way.

cards.statement: In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking a bit less alcohol went with slightly less heart disease, not more.

questions: Do heavy drinking days change the heart risk?

lines.short: Heavy drinking days went with more heart disease than drinking the same amount evenly.
lines.but: This comes from one team's review of seven studies, and it does not say what counted as heavy.
how: One team pooled seven studies of people who drank under 30 grams of alcohol a day on average.
Compared with people who had never drunk, those without heavy days had about a third lower heart risk. Those with heavy days had no lower risk.
The team's earlier review pointed the same way.
Genes that lower drinking also lower heavy drinking, so critics say gene studies cannot tell the two apart.

questions: Does drinking raise the risk of stroke?

lines.short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
lines.but: For small amounts it is less clear: older studies found slightly fewer strokes, but the Chinese gene study did not.
how: In a study of more than 160,000 Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes. The risk rose steadily with the amount.
For each extra 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day), bleeding strokes were almost a fifth more common, and strokes from blocked vessels about a tenth more common.
Women in China, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes. Most gene studies of people of European descent found the same direction.
Older studies comparing people who drink with people who don't found more strokes at high amounts, but no difference overall.

cards.statement: In gene studies, drinking more went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.

questions: Does drinking raise blood pressure?

lines.short: People whose genes made them drink more had higher blood pressure.
lines.but: The studies do not say how many more people out of 100 get high blood pressure.
how: In a Chinese study, men's top blood-pressure number was about 4 points higher for each extra 40 grams of alcohol a day that their genes predicted.
Asking the men how much they drank gave about the same rise.
In European studies, people with a gene that makes them drink a little less had slightly lower blood pressure and less high blood pressure, most clearly among heavier drinkers.
That gene also went with lower blood pressure in people who said they didn't drink, so it may act in other ways too.

questions: Does drinking raise the risk of other heart and blood-vessel problems?

lines.short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more narrowed leg arteries; other results were unclear.
lines.but: These results come from two studies using the same UK volunteers, with few cases of some problems.
how: Two gene studies used data from UK Biobank, a large study of UK volunteers.
Genes for drinking more went with more narrowed arteries, mostly in the legs, even after allowing for genes linked to smoking.
In one study, links with an irregular heartbeat and a swollen main artery became unclear after allowing for those smoking genes. The other study found a link with an irregular heartbeat.
For heart failure the two studies disagreed. For blood clots in the veins, no clear link was found, but one could not be ruled out.

questions: Does drinking alcohol raise the risk of cancer?

lines.short: More drinking went with more mouth, throat, gullet, bowel, liver and breast cancer than not drinking.
lines.but: These studies watched groups of people, and about half did not take smoking or other differences into account.
how: A review pooled 572 studies of almost half a million people with cancer. It compared people who drank with people who did not drink.

At more than four drinks a day (a drink here is 12.5 g of alcohol), mouth and throat cancer and one type of gullet cancer were about 5 times as common. Breast cancer was about 1.6 times as common, and bowel cancer about 1.4 times. The bowel cancer link was clear in men but not in women.
Kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were less common in people who drank. For the lymph glands, the authors think some people cut down when they first feel ill.
The review gives no numbers out of 100, and it did not check the quality of the studies. An international cancer agency judges that alcohol causes these cancers; this review alone cannot show it.

cards.statement: In a big review, more drinking went with more breast cancer, as well as mouth, throat and liver cancer.

questions: Does drinking a little raise the risk of cancer?

lines.short: Compared with not drinking, up to one drink a day went with slightly more of some cancers, fewer of others.
lines.but: The differences are so small that errors in reporting drinking, or other differences between the groups, could explain them.
how: A review of 572 studies compared people who had up to 12.5 g of alcohol a day, about one drink, with people who did not drink.
Breast cancer was 1.04 times as common, and one type of gullet cancer 1.26 times. Mouth and throat cancer was 1.13 times as common, but not in studies that followed people over time.
Lung, kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were a little less common in people who had up to one drink a day.
People who drink more sometimes report less, and some people counted as not drinking had stopped. Small results like these can come from such errors. The review gives no numbers out of 100.

questions: How many cancers are caused by alcohol?

lines.short: A model estimated that drinking caused about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
lines.but: It is a computer estimate, not a count. It applies risks from studies of groups of people to every country.
how: Researchers combined how much people drink in each country with cancer risks from earlier studies. They compared this with a world where no one had ever drunk.
They estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer made up the most.
Most were linked to more than 20 g of alcohol a day, about two drinks. About 103,000 were linked to less than that.
The model counted only harms, for the cancers an international agency lists. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths from alcohol in 2004.

cards.statement: Drinking alcohol was estimated to cause about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.

questions: How much drinking raises the risk of liver cirrhosis?

lines.short: The more people drank, the higher their cirrhosis risk, compared with people who did not drink.
lines.but: How much the risk rose differed a lot between studies, and drinking was asked about only once.
how: In a Danish study of 55,917 people aged 50 to 64, about 1 in 100 men and 3 in 1,000 women got alcohol-related cirrhosis over about 15 years.

A review of 9 studies, mostly counting deaths from cirrhosis, compared people who drank with people who did not. A drink here is 12 g of alcohol. At two drinks a day the risk was about 3 times as high, and at seven or more about 11 times (from 4 studies).
At seven or more drinks a day, studies of men found from about 2 times to 22 times the risk.
At up to about two drinks a day, results disagree: some found a rise, some none, and some studies of men even found less cirrhosis.

questions: Is the cirrhosis risk from drinking different for women and men?

lines.short: At the same amount, studies found a bigger rise in cirrhosis risk for women than for men.
lines.but: No study tested the difference, and much of the evidence on women comes from one old American study.
how: Each figure compares people who drank with people of the same sex who did not drink, or drank little.

At about five drinks a day (48 to 60 g), studies of cirrhosis deaths found 14.7 times the risk for women and 7.0 times for men. In a newer review and a Danish study, the gap was within the margins of error.
In a Danish study, fewer women than men got alcohol-related cirrhosis (19 against 66 in 100,000 a year), but the women drank less.
No study gave the risk, out of 100, for women and men who drink the same amount.

questions: For the same amount, is drinking every day worse for the liver?

lines.short: In one study, men who drank daily had more cirrhosis than men drinking 2 to 4 days a week.
lines.but: People who drank daily also drank more, and the study could not fully separate how often from how much.
how: The study followed 55,917 people aged 50 to 64 for about 15 years. It asked once how often and how much they drank.
After taking into account how much they drank, smoking, schooling and waist size, men who drank every day had 3.7 times the risk of men who drank on 2 to 4 days a week.
Women showed no clear pattern. A review reported that, in a large British study of women, daily drinking was linked to 1.6 times the risk.
The study could not look at drinking a lot on a few days (binge drinking).

questions: How common is alcohol use disorder?

lines.short: In a US survey, 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year.
lines.but: Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.
how: Alcohol use disorder is found with a list of 11 signs of problem drinking: 2 or more in a year count. In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked 36,309 adults set questions to find it.
About 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year, and 29 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild. It was most common at ages 18 to 29: about 27 in 100.
The survey's authors think it became more common after 2001. We think their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
The survey missed people who were homeless or in prison, and most people in treatment. For the world, a review passes on an estimate of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older.

cards.statement: In one US survey, alcohol use disorder was most common in people over 65.
In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.

questions: How many people with alcohol use disorder get help?

lines.short: In a US survey, 20 in 100 people who ever had it sought help.
lines.but: People said this themselves, and the survey left out most people who were in treatment.
how: In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked people with alcohol use disorder whether they had ever looked for treatment or help.
About 20 in 100 who had ever had it said yes, and about 8 in 100 of those who had it in the past year.
Groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous were the most common kind of help. People with severe disorder looked for help more often: about 35 in 100, against 4 in 100 with mild disorder.
A review passes on about 22 in 100 for Europe and the world, but these count people who got treatment, not people who looked for it.

cards.statement: In a US survey, most people who had ever had alcohol use disorder had looked for help.

questions: What are the DTs (delirium tremens), and how often do they happen?

lines.short: Sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal; a few in 100 people in hospital get it.
lines.but: Most figures are passed on by one review or come from old trials, mostly one from 1969.
how: The DTs are confusion that comes on fast and comes and goes, together with signs of withdrawal such as shaking or a fast pulse.
A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after withdrawal begins and last 2 or 3 days. It says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them.
In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who got dummy pills developed delirium. Most of these people were in one trial from 1969.
The review says about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. It names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs they are more likely.

cards.statement: A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after alcohol withdrawal begins.
Most people treated in hospital for alcohol withdrawal get the DTs (sudden confusion).

questions: Does talking therapy add anything to naltrexone for alcohol problems?

lines.short: In one large trial, adding talking therapy to naltrexone did not help more.
lines.but: It was one US trial, not built to test combinations.
how: 1,383 adults who had just stopped drinking got naltrexone, acamprosate, both or dummy pills, with or without up to 20 sessions of therapy. Everyone taking pills also had 9 short check-ins with a health worker.
Naltrexone with therapy did no better than either one alone. On days without alcohol, only naltrexone without therapy was clearly better than dummy pills.
With dummy pills, adding therapy was linked to more days without alcohol in one comparison.
People who had therapy without pills or check-ins had fewer days without alcohol. In the year after, no difference between the groups was clear.

cards.statement: In a large trial, naltrexone plus talking therapy worked much better than either one alone.

questions: How many pregnant women drink alcohol?

lines.short: About 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide drank some alcohol. By region, from under 1 to 25.
lines.but: Most countries had too few studies, so a model filled them in. Women may not report all drinking.
how: Researchers pooled 328 studies from 50 countries, published from 1984 to 2014. In them, pregnant women or new mothers said if they drank.
Only 29 countries had enough studies to pool. For the other 158, a model worked out a number from the country's income, how much its women drink, and its region.
In each WHO world region, out of 100 pregnant women: African 10. Americas 11. Eastern Mediterranean under 1. European 25. South-East Asia 2. Western Pacific 9.
Groups who may drink more, such as teenagers or women with an alcohol use disorder, were left out. How much and when women drank was not studied.

cards.statement: In one estimate, about 25 in 100 pregnant women in the European region drank some alcohol.

questions: How common are fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) and fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS)?

lines.short: About 8 in 1,000 children are thought to have FASD. About 1.5 in 1,000 people have FAS.
lines.but: Few countries had counted it. Most numbers were worked out from how many women said they drank.
how: FASD is the name for the effects of alcohol on a child before birth. It covers several diagnoses, and FAS is one of them.
Researchers found 24 studies in 8 countries that looked for FASD in children. Results ranged from under 1 to about 208 in 1,000, by place and method.

For most countries there was no count. The team took the estimated share of women who drank in pregnancy and divided it by one fixed number. In the regions with the lowest figures, no study had counted it.
That number is an average from a few countries. It is not the chance for any one pregnancy. Ways to diagnose FASD also differ.

questions: How did doctors first spot fetal alcohol syndrome?

lines.short: In 1973, doctors described 8 children of mothers who drank heavily. All grew poorly and developed slowly.
lines.but: Some children were picked because they had these signs. They were not compared with other children.
how: A team in Seattle, USA, examined 8 children: 5 girls and 3 boys from three ethnic groups, aged 3 months to almost 5 years when tested.
All 8 were small before and after birth and did not catch up. All had short eye openings and were behind in development. Seven had small heads.
Many also had a small upper jaw (7 children), unusual palm creases (6), joint problems (5) or heart problems (5). The paper did not yet use the name fetal alcohol syndrome.
Milder cases were left out, and how much the mothers drank was not recorded. Four of six mothers with a record lost weight in pregnancy, and the study could not separate nutrition from alcohol.

questions: How much of a ketamine dose reaches the blood, and how fast?

lines.short: Nearly all of an injected dose reaches the blood. Swallowed, only about a sixth does.
lines.but: Both figures come from four people each, in one study from 1982.
how: Healthy volunteers were given ketamine three ways on different days, with blood tests each time.
Each person's own dose into a vein was the yardstick for the other two ways.
Into a muscle, about 93 parts in 100 reached the blood; swallowed, about 17 in 100.
A later study of three men found about the same, but they swallowed a tablet, not a drink.

questions: How much ketamine reaches the blood by nose, tongue or suppository?

lines.short: In three men, the nose spray reached the blood best, then tongue and suppository.
lines.but: Only three men took part, and two of the methods were not carried out as described.
how: Three healthy men tried five forms of ketamine, a week or more apart, with blood tests.
Against a dose into a vein: nose spray about 45 in 100, tongue tablet and suppository about 30 in 100.
The men swallowed the tablets that were meant to stay under the tongue.
The suppository results differed so much between the three men that the average says little.

questions: What do brain scans show while someone is given ketamine?

lines.short: In scans, brain activity went up, not down, most of all at the front.
lines.but: The scans show one session only, and cannot show which brain change causes which feeling.
how: Ten healthy people were scanned with and without ketamine, each person compared with themselves.
Whole-brain energy use rose about a quarter, and it rose in every single person.
A 2024 summary of 33 imaging studies found the clearest agreement at one spot near the front.
One mirror-image form of ketamine, called R, moved the other way and lowered energy use.

cards.statement: Brain scans show that ketamine turns overall brain activity down.

questions: Does ketamine affect memory and thinking that night, and 3 days later?

lines.short: That night, memory scores were far below other partygoers'. Three days later the gap was mostly gone.
lines.but: Two small studies by one team, and nobody tested what people had taken.
how: People were tested within half an hour of taking ketamine. They remembered less than half as much of a short story as people at the party who had not taken it.
They felt strongly cut off from their body and surroundings, numb, and as if time had changed.
Three days later, at home, their attention scores matched the other group's, and most of these feelings had gone. In one of the two studies, feeling detached was still higher.
Some memory scores were still lower. People may have remembered little of the first test, so had less practice. Or the groups were different to begin with.

questions: Does memory improve when people cut down or stop frequent ketamine use?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. People who had stopped did as well as people who don't use it.
lines.but: The people who had stopped had mostly used less, and nobody was tested before starting.
how: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well on memory tests as people who don't use ketamine. They still did a year later.
But most of them had used less than the people who used most days, so this does not show that stopping fixed anything.
In 18 people who had cut down, one word test caught up after 3 to 4 years. Story memory and speed stayed lower, as at their first test.
People who were still using also scored better on average a year later, perhaps partly from practice.

cards.statement: People who've quit ketamine do worse on memory tests than people who don't use it.

questions: Is using ketamine often linked to low mood, feeling detached or unusual beliefs?

lines.short: People who used ketamine most days more often reported unusual beliefs, feeling detached or feeling low.
lines.but: Mostly mild. Nobody was asked before they started, so the cause is not known.
how: A London team asked three groups: people who used ketamine more than four times a week, people who used other drugs, and people who used none.
The frequent group reported more unusual beliefs. In daily life, they also more often felt cut off from themselves or the world around them.
Their low-mood scores were a little higher, at most mild to moderate on average. A year later the scores had gone up.
More of them had family members with mental illness. That may matter too.

cards.statement: In a London study, people who used ketamine most days more often felt cut off from themselves in daily life.

questions: Is using cannabis in pregnancy linked to a smaller baby, early birth or intensive care?
Is cannabis in pregnancy linked to smaller babies or intensive care?

lines.short: Babies were a bit lighter, and more of them went to intensive care after birth.
lines.but: Many mothers also smoked or drank. Most studies could not tell this apart from cannabis.
how: Researchers combined 19 studies, mostly from before 2000. They compared babies of mothers who did and did not use cannabis while pregnant.
Babies of mothers who used cannabis weighed about 109 grams less. More of them went to newborn intensive care.
It is not clear whether they were born early more often. Birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common.
Most studies did not keep tobacco and alcohol apart from cannabis. So they cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.

cards.statement: Babies whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy went to newborn intensive care more often.

questions: Do cannabis medicines ease muscle stiffness in multiple sclerosis (MS)?

lines.short: People felt a little less stiff than with a dummy, but doctors' tests showed no clear change.
lines.but: The trials were short, most often tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with MS got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
On the medicine, people rated their stiffness a little lower. The gap was about three quarters of a point.
Doctors' stiffness ratings did not clearly change. Neither did daily activities or walking speed.
Most trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, for 15 weeks or less.

questions: Do cannabis medicines help with sickness from chemotherapy?

lines.short: In three small trials, more people had their sickness fully controlled than with a dummy.
lines.but: Only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined three trials. People having chemotherapy got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
About 47 in 100 people on the medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on the dummy.
Most other trials compared cannabis medicines with other sickness medicines. The review says these leaned towards cannabis too. But it did not combine them.
23 of the 28 trials had serious weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

cards.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.

questions: Does cannabis cause psychosis, or could something else explain the link?

lines.short: Not known. Part of the link seems to come from other differences between people.
lines.but: The gene studies only looked at ever trying cannabis, not at daily or strong use.
how: In seven big studies, taking other differences between people into account shrank the link by about half, on average.
In a Swedish study of relatives, the link got smaller the more closely related two people were. It was still there in identical twins, but nobody checked whether that could be chance.
Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with trying cannabis. Evidence that genes linked to trying cannabis go with schizophrenia was weaker.
The researchers who did these studies, and experts reading them, disagree about whether cannabis itself raises the risk.

cards.statement: Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with trying cannabis.

questions: Has schizophrenia become more common as more people used cannabis?

lines.short: Studies disagree: some places saw more psychosis over time, others no rise as use grew.
lines.but: We know these studies only through reviews, and changes in diagnosis can blur trends.
how: In Australia, a study found no clear rise in psychosis after cannabis use went up in the 1980s and 1990s.
In south-east London and in Zurich, psychosis became more common in people born more recently.
A review says that in the UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise.
Even if cannabis played a part, the rise would be small and hard to see in health records.

cards.statement: A review says UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise.

questions: Do drug and alcohol problems develop faster in women than in men?

lines.short: Not shown for women in general. It was seen mostly in people in treatment.
lines.but: All these studies rest on memory. People said years later how old they were at each step.
how: The idea came mostly from people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous. Years later, they had to say when each step came.

In two US treatment studies, some of women's steps looked 1 to 5 years shorter. In one, women started getting drunk regularly about 4 years later than men but reached their worst drinking at the same age.
In big US surveys of adults, fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Those who did got there about as fast as men: about 6 years after their first drink.
Among people with a cannabis problem in a US survey, women got there about 5 months sooner after first use than men. A review said 2.5 years, which is wrong.

cards.statement: In big US surveys, women who became dependent on alcohol got there faster than men did.

questions: Are women less likely than men to get alcohol or drug treatment?

lines.short: For alcohol, somewhat less likely, mostly years after problems start. For drugs, about the same.
lines.but: The surveys are from the US, and people remembered dates years later.
how: In US surveys from 1991 to 2002, men with alcohol dependence got treatment more often or sooner than women in some age groups.
In a 1992 survey, as a review describes it, 23 in 100 men and 15 in 100 women with alcohol problems had ever been treated. The gap appeared only 8 or more years after the problems began.
For drug problems, and for treatment in the past year, reviews describe no difference. In 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment got it.
Women more often went to mental health services. Reviews list barriers such as childcare and fear of losing custody, but several surveys found few differences in the barriers women and men named.

cards.statement: In the US, women with drug problems were much less likely than men to get treatment.

questions: In drug or alcohol treatment, do women do as well as men?

lines.short: Most large studies found no difference between women and men once in treatment.
lines.but: This comes from two reviews by one research group; we have not read the studies themselves.
how: Two reviews by one research group looked at many studies of people who had already started treatment. They did not check how good the studies were.
In large studies, women and men mostly stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Finding no difference does not prove the results are the same.
Where differences appeared, the older review found women mostly did better. The newer one found more cases where women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines.
Women-only programmes gave mixed results. In the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones, and did less well than a costlier hospital one.

cards.statement: Most large studies found that women do worse than men once in treatment.

questions: How often do people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis?

lines.short: On average, about 3 in 4 also used alcohol, and 4 to 6 in 10 cannabis.
lines.but: These averages mix very different studies, from about 1 in 10 to nearly all.
how: A review put together 16 counts of people who used cocaine, mostly from the US.
On average, about 3 in 4 had used alcohol on the same occasion or in the same period, and 4 to 6 in 10 had used cannabis.
None of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis (two left out recent cannabis use), so their results may mix up different drugs.
Animal studies almost never gave a second drug, so they did not copy how people use cocaine.

cards.statement: None of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis.

questions: Can caffeine bring on panic attacks in people with panic disorder?

lines.short: About half had a panic attack after one big dose; none after a dummy.
lines.but: Most studies used one large amount. The review cannot show what ordinary smaller servings do.
how: A 2022 review included 10 small lab studies of adults with panic disorder during a break from psychiatric medicines.
After caffeine, 121 of 237 had a panic attack. None was reported after a dummy drink or capsule, though not everyone completed both conditions.
In studies with both groups, about 54 in 100 people with panic disorder had an attack after caffeine, against 2 in 100 without it.
Anxiety also rose more after caffeine than a dummy in all five studies that tested that comparison. The pooled anxiety result was a different comparison: change after caffeine in the two groups.

cards.statement: Caffeine can set off panic attacks in people with panic disorder.

questions: Does eating before drinking change blood alcohol?

lines.short: In 9 men, a meal just before drinking roughly halved peak blood alcohol.
lines.but: One small lab study of young men. It measured blood alcohol, without testing impairment.
how: Nine healthy young men were given the same small amount of alcohol on five days: after three kinds of breakfast, after a night without food, or through a drip.
After a breakfast, the highest blood alcohol was about half the level after no food: 13 to 18 against 31 mg per 100 ml.
The kind of breakfast made no clear difference, but the study was too small to tell.
After food, blood alcohol varied more from person to person. Larger amounts, women and other meals were not studied.

questions: Do official counts miss drug deaths?

lines.short: Some deaths are missing; others are counted without showing which drug was involved.
lines.but: The gaps differ by place and rules. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.
how: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 out of 100 overdoses had only an unspecified-drug code.
Models guessed which drugs those counted deaths involved. They did not find deaths missing from the total.
In Stockholm, lists with similar totals disagreed about which people to include. They used different rules.
An England and Wales estimate suggests counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It did not match each death across lists.

cards.statement: Official records name the drug involved in nearly every overdose death.

questions: Do official counts miss heroin deaths?

lines.short: In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than records did.
lines.but: Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.
how: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine. Some death records said morphine or mixed drugs instead of heroin.
In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 52 in 100 of the deaths a fuller review linked to heroin.

In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), about 34 in 100 deaths a review linked to heroin lacked the heroin code in national figures. A few deaths coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance.
In England and Wales, an estimate came out about half as large again as the official count. It mixed heroin with morphine and did not match each death.

cards.statement: In Maryland, death certificates named heroin in almost every death a fuller review linked to heroin.
A death record can say morphine even when the person took heroin.

questions: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths?

lines.short: Sometimes: at one centre, about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause.
lines.but: Only two US places have been studied, so other places may differ.
how: At a North Carolina autopsy centre (2016 to 2021), 2,719 deaths were thought to be drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 10 in 100 had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs. In some, the tests found no drug at all.
It went the other way too. Of 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs, drug tests showed that about 49 in 100 were.

In Alabama, three doctors were told everything about 60 chosen deaths except what the autopsy found inside the body. Their cause of death matched the autopsy doctor's in 67 to 80 of every 100. They did not always agree with each other either.
In 2018, about 11 in 100 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug tests. Small offices had them less often than big ones.

cards.statement: About 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths at one US autopsy centre had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs.
At one US autopsy centre, deaths nobody thought were from drugs almost never turned out to be drug deaths.

questions: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs (the 'gateway' idea)?

lines.short: Not known. Cannabis usually comes first, but that does not prove it leads on.
lines.but: Shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain the cannabis link.
how: In New Zealand, at least 86 in 100 young people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before.
Australian twins grew up together. The one starting cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100.
A computer model where cannabis did nothing still made the same pattern. Some people were likelier to use any drug, and were offered cannabis first.
Experts disagreed about the New Zealand cannabis link. One said hidden factors no longer explain it away; another said factors changing with age still could.

cards.statement: A computer model gave cannabis no effect at all. Yet people in it still mostly used cannabis first.
In one twin study, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants.

questions: Are cocaine deaths more common in hot weather, and why?

lines.short: In 1990s New York, hot days had about a third more cocaine overdose deaths.
lines.but: The study compared days, not people, and did not allow for season.
how: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, there were 2.34 cocaine overdose deaths a day on hot days and 1.76 on other days.

Deaths in the opiate group, where cocaine was absent or present only in amounts judged clinically insignificant, did not clearly rise. The study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine.

In a lab, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were warmed in a heated suit after one small dose. They began to sweat later, warmed up more and felt less hot than after a numbing drug used for comparison.
The lab study used one small dose in people at rest, so it may not match real use in hot weather.

cards.statement: In 1990s New York, cocaine overdose deaths were more common on hot days.
In a lab, people given cocaine felt less hot in a heated suit, even though their bodies warmed up more.

questions: How is a death counted as a drug death?

lines.short: Different lists use different rules, so they do not always count the same deaths.
lines.but: The matching studies cover three places. The newest linked data are from 2012.
how: Some lists count drug poisoning as the main cause. Others count drugs found in tests, with age limits.
One death can be counted under several drugs. Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death.
About 49 out of 100 people were on both lists in Norway. Fewer than half were on both in Sweden.
In New Mexico, about 89 out of 100 were on both lists. This study included other poisons too.

cards.statement: If a drug is found in someone's body after death, that shows the drug caused the death.
There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.

questions: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates?

lines.short: Not clear. Coroner areas recorded deaths less precisely, but switching showed no clear change.
lines.but: No study checked which records were right, and the study of switching used data up to 1998.
how: In the US, medical examiners are usually doctors appointed to the job. Coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training.

In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state.
Other US studies found that death certificates named no drug more often where coroners work.
But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement.

cards.statement: In some US states, coroners, who are often elected, need no medical training.

questions: Can a blood level show that a drug caused death?

lines.short: Not on its own. Levels overlap between deaths with different causes.
lines.but: The rules and tests used to decide the cause also affect the comparison.
how: In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in drug deaths overlapped with levels in injury deaths.
An older review reports a similar overlap for morphine. It also cites comparisons with people who survived an overdose.
Finnish data compare blood after death with treatment ranges, not the same people before and after death.
At one US centre, full autopsy changed suspected drug-death classifications in both directions. This study tested drug presence, not levels.

cards.statement: In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in drug deaths overlapped with MDMA levels in deaths from injuries.

questions: Do stimulant medicines help people stop using cocaine?

lines.short: In nine trials up to 2006, they did no better than a dummy pill.
lines.but: The trials were small, and newer reviews of these medicines have not been read yet.
how: Nine trials gave 640 people with cocaine dependence a stimulant medicine or a dummy pill. Everyone also had talking therapy.
There was no clear difference in staying in treatment or in urine tests positive for cocaine, but the trials were too small to rule out a modest benefit.
About 4 in 100 stopped the medicine because of unwanted effects, against about 1 in 100 on the dummy pill. The commonest were trouble sleeping, anxiety and feeling jittery.
One extra analysis found fewer positive tests with dexamphetamine, but it leans on filled-in results and on one group in which 42 of 46 people dropped out.

questions: Why do people take ketamine, and what do they want from it?

lines.short: Most said: for its effects, like melting into their surroundings, and for fun.
lines.but: These 202 people were not picked at random, so their reasons may not be everyone's.
how: In Sydney in 1998 and 1999, 62 in 100 people said they first took ketamine for its effect, and 25 in 100 because friends did. In London, 81 in 100 said they were offered some and enjoyed it, and 17 in 100 that they wanted to forget their troubles.

The best parts named in Sydney were changed senses (78 in 100) and feeling outside the body (52 in 100). The worst was fear of the 'K-hole', a state of feeling deeply cut off (45 in 100). In London, 72 in 100 liked feeling they melted into their surroundings, and half disliked memory problems.

In London, the places most named were a friend's house (84 in 100) and home (71 in 100), more than clubs (52 in 100). In long interviews with 12 people in England, fun came first: some wanted a mild, chatty feeling, others a strong one.

Some people feel little from an amount. Reasons given here were tolerance and a weaker product: 22 in 100 in Sydney needed more for the same effect. In England, people said an unwanted K-hole came mostly from taking more than they meant to. Some sought one out.

cards.statement: In a Sydney study, most said they first took ketamine because friends did.
In a London study, more people had taken ketamine at home than in clubs.

questions: Does cocaine narrow heart arteries, and do beta-blockers make it worse?

lines.short: Yes, in a lab cocaine narrowed heart arteries a little. After a beta-blocker, blood flow fell further in all 10 patients, but its effect on heart attacks is unknown.
lines.but: No trial has ever tested beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine.
how: That lab test used 10 heart patients who had never used cocaine. The beta-blocker, propranolol, went straight into a heart artery.
In 2008, US heart doctors advised against beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine. That rests mainly on small lab tests, animal tests and expert opinion.
In hospital records of about 2,000 people, heart attacks and deaths were not clearly different with beta-blockers. But doctors chose who got them.
Two reviews counted one cocaine study's blood tests as heart attacks or damage. That study of 58 people reported no heart complications or deaths.

cards.statement: The warning against beta-blockers after cocaine is based on big trials.
After cocaine, a beta-blocker improves blood flow to the heart.

questions: How many UK deaths were linked to ketamine, and what were they?

lines.short: In England, ketamine was found or named in 283 deaths from 1999 to 2019, about 30 a year lately. Most had other drugs found too.
lines.but: Finding ketamine after a death does not show it caused the death.
how: A national register counted deaths in England where coroners' records named ketamine or tests found it. The rest of the UK wasn't included.
On average, 4 to 5 drugs were found. Records linked only ketamine to 32 deaths; it was the only drug found in 14 of those.
An earlier count by the same team found 23 UK deaths with ketamine from 1993 to 2006. It was the only drug found in 4.
About 3 in 4 deaths were recorded as accidental poisoning. 16 were suicides; others included drownings, falls and road crashes.

cards.statement: In UK deaths linked to ketamine, other drugs were always found too.

questions: Does coffee dehydrate you?

lines.short: Not in a 3-day test. Men who drink coffee daily peed 2.41 litres a day on coffee days and 2.43 on water days.
lines.but: One 3-day test in 50 men who already drank coffee daily, too small to rule out a small effect.
how: In Birmingham, UK, 50 healthy men who drink coffee daily had coffee for 3 days. Another time, they had the same amount of water instead.
Their food and other drinks were the same both times, so only the coffee changed.
Urine strength, blood tests and body weight did not differ. The one difference: a little more salt in the urine on coffee.
A coffee research institute paid for it, and body water results were shown for only 25 of the 50 men.

cards.statement: In a 3-day test, men who drink coffee daily peed much more on coffee days than on water days.

questions: Do benzodiazepines cause dementia?

lines.short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.
lines.but: Neither study could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions.
how: In Quebec records, 50 in 100 older people with Alzheimer's had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 without it.
The link appeared only with longer use. The records often missed why the pills were taken, and held nothing on education, smoking or drinking.
A Seattle study tested 3,434 older people every 2 years. About 3 in 100 a year got dementia, with the heaviest use or none.
A small extra risk showed up with light or moderate use, not the heaviest. The authors say early dementia symptoms may explain it.

cards.statement: Studies have shown that benzodiazepines cause dementia.
Taking benzodiazepines for a long time has been shown to cause dementia.

questions: Does alcohol kill brain cells?

lines.short: In one study, men who drank alcohol heavily for years had about as many nerve cells in the brain's outer layer as other men: about 23 billion each.
lines.but: Only the outer layer was counted, in 22 men, so it can't say what heavy drinking does to other areas.
how: In Denmark, scientists counted nerve cells in brains after death. 11 men had drunk alcohol heavily for years; 11 others had not.
Both groups had about 23 billion. The numbers rule out a loss bigger than about 1 in 10 in the men who drank heavily.
Only 11 of 55 brains were used. Men who had had the DTs, withdrawal fits or an alcohol-related brain illness were left out.
The brain's wiring (white matter) was not clearly smaller with heavy drinking; only its share of brain weight was lower.

cards.statement: In one study, men who drank alcohol heavily for years had fewer nerve cells in the brain's outer layer than other men.

questions: Is moderate drinking linked to changes in the brain?

lines.short: In one UK study, people who drank more alcohol more often had a memory area rated 'shrunken' on a scan. So did 35 in 100 who barely drank.
lines.but: Each brain was scanned once, so the study shows a link, not shrinking, and not that alcohol caused it.
how: 527 UK government workers, mostly men, reported how much alcohol they drank over 30 years, then had one brain scan around age 70.
'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. Even 35 in 100 people who barely drank alcohol got that rating.
The paper's 'three times the odds' came from the top of its 'moderate' range for men; lower down, the study was too small to tell.
Only one of three thinking tests (naming words that start with a letter) fell slightly faster with more drinking. No test at the scan differed.

cards.statement: A UK study scanned people's brains over 30 years and saw them shrink as people drank more alcohol.
In a UK scan study, 35 in 100 people who barely drank had a memory area rated 'shrunken'.

questions: Is drinking coffee linked to better or worse health?

lines.short: Mostly better: in studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often. In pregnancy, and for women's bones, the links went the other way.
lines.but: These studies only watched people, and gene studies found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.
how: A big review gathered the research on coffee and health. Most of it came from studies that followed people for years.
People who drank coffee had lower rates of death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and, most of all, liver disease.
In pregnancy, more coffee was linked to low birth weight and losing the pregnancy. Women who drank more had more fractures; men had fewer.
A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked; people who smoke tend to drink more coffee.

cards.statement: In studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often.
Drinking coffee raises your risk of lung cancer.

questions: Do supervised injection sites reduce overdose deaths?

lines.short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.
lines.but: Just one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.
how: Coroners recorded 290 overdose deaths from illegal drugs in Vancouver, 2001 to 2005. About half involved opioids, and about 6 in 10 cocaine.
Within 500 metres: 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before it opened in 2003, 33 in the 2.3 after, about 6 fewer a year.
Critics blamed extra police from April 2003. The authors said that crackdown ended within weeks of the opening.
Critics also blamed the study's start in 2001, a year with more heroin around. The two papers they cited show overdoses falling since the late 1990s, but neither measured heroin's strength or price.

cards.statement: A study proved that Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs cut overdose deaths nearby.
Overdoses were already falling years before Vancouver's injection site opened.
